articles.title: FACT CHECK: No death penalty for Filipina arrested in Hong Kong for drug trafficking
articles.summary: The death penalty has long been abolished in Hong Kong

blocks.text: Claim: The Filipino woman arrested in Hong Kong for illegal possession of drugs may be executed by hanging.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim was made in a post by the Facebook page “JIL Review TV” on November 8. The page currently has over 130,000 followers.
As of writing, it has received 3,800 reactions, 1,600 comments, and 150 shares.
Text on the post reads, “BREAKING: Posibleng bibitayin ang Pinay na nahulihan ng cocaine sa HK.”
(BREAKING: Filipina caught with cocaine in Hong Kong faces possible execution.)

The facts: Capital punishment, whether by hanging or any other method of execution, is not legal in Hong Kong. The death penalty was formally abolished through the Crimes (Amendment) Ordinance in 1993, with the last execution carried out in November 1966.

The false claim stemmed from reports that a 22-year-old Filipino woman arriving from Phnom Penh was arrested in Hong Kong on October 31 for suspected drug trafficking. During customs clearance protocols, about 6 kilograms of suspected cocaine with an estimated market value of about HK$3.6 million was found in her suitcase.
Under Hong Kong’s Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, drug trafficking carries a maximum penalty upon conviction of a fine of $5 million and life imprisonment.

The Filipina was charged with one count of trafficking in a dangerous drug and her case was set to be brought to the West Kowloon Magistrates’ Court on November 2. As of writing, there are no updates on the court’s ruling on her case.

Recent drug busts: The case follows other recently reported drug trafficking cases. On October 1, a major drug bust happened in Laos, where a private jet carrying 521 kilos of suspected shabu worth P3.5 billion was intercepted. It was reportedly bound for Manila. (READ: Inside story: Politician behind 521-kilo shabu shipment bound for Manila)
On October 17, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said 11 persons of interest are linked to the shipment, including a former Bangsamoro Parliament member.
A Filipino, Fahad Mulok Dibarosan, was arrested in the Laos drug bust. Authorities said they will appeal to commute a possible death sentence for the arrested Filipino.

In a separate incident, Thai authorities intercepted about 1,178 kilograms of suspected shabu aboard a fishing vessel in the Gulf of Thailand in early October. Authorities later said there was no evidence indicating that the shipment was bound for the Philippines. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

articles.title: [OPINION] Manny Pacquiao, anti-poverty chief, can give up some privileges
articles.summary: Start with dropping police escorts. True leadership for the marginalized requires sharing the everyday struggles and lines of ordinary citizens.

blocks.text: The lobby drop-off at the Dusit Thani Davao stopped moving a little after 2 pm on October 27. Cars backed up along the driveway. People in lanyards drifted toward the glass doors and craned their necks to see what was holding everyone up.

Under the portico, a man was suiting up. He had changed into a racing jersey and pulled a black balaclava over his head, a red gaiter at his throat. He tugged his collar into place beside a big adventure motorbike, a black helmet resting on his top box. A broad man in a black polo cap stood at his elbow. Behind them, an officer of the Philippine National Police Highway Patrol Group sat on his own bike in a white helmet, waiting to clear the road.

The man in the balaclava was Manny Pacquiao, who was appointed the lead convenor of the National Anti-Poverty Commission (NAPC) with a rank of Cabinet secretary in September. Earlier that day, he had been inside the ballroom talking about poverty. He is, after all, the man in charge of it.

Inside, at the Mindanao Development Forum, Pacquiao had told a room of officials and investors that “development must reach the people, not just the places where investments are made.” It was a good line. He also admitted, with what sounded like honesty, that many Filipinos don’t know his agency exists.

The NAPC was created in 1998 under the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act. It doesn’t build houses or hand out cash. Its job is to coordinate poverty programs across national agencies, local governments, and the private sector, monitor whether they work, recommend policy, and make sure the poor themselves have a voice in it.
It is, in other words, the government’s conscience on poverty. It is supposed to be the office that asks whether all the other offices are reaching the people they claim to serve.

Malacañang cited Pacquiao’s desire to help people in marginalized sectors. Nobody doubts the story behind that. He grew up poor in Mindanao, and for years he handed out cash to long lines of Filipinos after his fights.
That is precisely why the scene under the portico stayed with me.

I don’t begrudge any public official his security. Threats are real, and a former senator and world champion draws crowds wherever he goes. The motorbike is his own business. I am not writing to scold a man for liking engines.

What stayed with me was the order of things. The lobby stopped. The car queue stopped. A police officer from the Highway Patrol Group, paid from public funds, waited to clear the road ahead. Everyone else was made to wait so that one man could pass. People craned to see, and then went back to waiting.

That is a small picture of a large problem. In much of this country, and especially in Mindanao, power is measured by who gets waved through. The mayor’s convoy, the governor’s escort, the politician whose car never seems to queue. We have grown so used to it that we think it’s normal. But it teaches the rest of us a lesson: that the road belongs first to those with guards, and the rest of us use it when they are done.

An anti-poverty secretary, of all officials, should feel the weight of that lesson. The people his agency exists to serve are the ones who are always made to wait: in the clinic line, at the municipal hall, at the checkpoint, on the shoulder of the highway while the convoy goes by. When the man in charge of poverty leaves a development forum behind a police escort, he is showing us, without meaning to, which side of the cleared road he is on.

The numbers he inherits look good on paper. The Philippines Statistics Authority reported that poverty incidence fell to 9.7% in 2025, or about 11.08 million Filipinos, down from 15.5% in 2023. It is the first time the figure dropped into single digits, three years ahead of the government’s target. (READ: [In This Economy] Less than 10% of Filipinos are now poor? Not so fast)

But the line that counts someone as poor is low. A typical family of five is not considered poor if it earns slightly more than P14,634 a month, which works out to about P96 per person per day. Think tanks such as IBON have called that standard outdated, and when Social Weather Stations ask families directly, self-rated poverty stood at 49% in June. One in 10 Filipinos is poor by the government’s count. Half say they are poor by their own.

The gap between those two numbers is where an anti-povery commission earns its keep. Its job is not to celebrate the official figure. It is to stand with the people who don’t recognize themselves in it, and ask why. That is hard to do from behind a cleared road.

To be fair, Pacquiao has been in the job barely two months, and the commission he leads coordinates other agencies’ programs rather than runs its own. He cannot fix poverty by himself, and nobody should expect him to. As a senator, he consistently backed bills to raise the minimum wage and proposed narrowing the pay gap between cities and the countryside. He knows hunger in a way most Cabinet secretaries never will. That is a real asset if he uses it.

To use it, he needs to make the commission loud. Publish, in plain language, which agencies’ anti-poverty programs are reaching people and which are not. Take the gap between the official poverty rate and what families say about their own lives, and make the commission’s central question. Go to the municipalities where the poorest Filipinos live and hold hearings where they can be heard, without the stage and the motorcade.

And, small as it sounds, wait in line. The most useful thing a powerful man can do for the powerless is to refuse, now and then, to be waved through. An anti-poverty secretary who queues like everyone would tell us more about his priorities than any speech.

When the escort finally moved, the Highway Patrol officer pulled out first, then the motorbike, then the men behind it. The road opened. The cars in the driveway inched forward, and the drop-off began to move again, one vehicle at a time.

Development, Pacquiao told us that morning, must reach the people. I believe he meant it. But development travels the way power travels, and that afternoon I watched how power travels in this country; covered, guarded, and with the road cleared ahead of it. The rest of us followed when it was gone.
If the man in charge of poverty wants development to reach the people, he could start by letting the people see him in the same line. – Rappler.com

Mick Basa is an investment analyst who tracks mergers and acquisitions (M&A) across Southeast Asia, focusing on Indonesia, and more recently, Thailand. He was Rappler’s business reporter in 2014 before moving to Indonesia.

articles.title: Dolores Huerta honored in ceremony at California state capitol
articles.summary:
Labor leader was remembered for her advocacy and co-founding union that would become United Farm Workers

California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most…

blocks.text: California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists, at a memorial ceremony Monday at the state capitol.

They remembered her as a relentless advocate for a more just and fair world. Huerta co-founded a union that became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez and made famous her rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” – which translates to “Yes, it can be done!”
Huerta, 96, died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California, last month. A celebration of life, with an interfaith memorial service, will be held in her hometown on Friday.

Robert Rivas, the Democratic assembly speaker, had called Huerta a family friend and mentor. Rivas’ grandfather, Servando Flores, moved from Mexico to California in the 1960s and went on to organize fellow farmworkers alongside Huerta.

blocks.caption: People pay their respects to Dolores Huerta at the California state capitol. Photograph: Jose Luis Villegas/AP

blocks.text: “She is the mother of our Latino civil rights movement,” Rivas said. “Her place in the history of our state and nation is enduring.”

Rivas stood beside fellow Democrats Xavier Becerra, the governor-elect, Monique Limón, the senate president pro tempore, and Nancy Pelosi, the former US House speaker, in the Ccapitol rotunda as they spoke about Huerta during an invitation-only ceremony. There were performances of songs that included We Shall Overcome and Put a Little Love in Your Heart before the space was opened to the public.

“As we honor one of the towering figures of our time, we make her this solemn promise: the march goes on,” said Limón, who is serving as acting governor while Gavin Newsom, the governor, is out of state.

Before the event began, Huerta’s casket was transported to the capitol by a hearse adorned with flags reading “Sí, se puede!” Hundreds of people, including union leaders, politicians and members of the public, followed behind, many with marigolds in hand.

blocks.caption: Maria Helena Chavez, daughter of Dolores Huerta and Richard Chavez, is comforted by her husband Rafael Rodriguez. Photograph: Héctor Amezcua/Reuters

blocks.text: Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930 and raised in California’s farm-rich San Joaquin valley. She became an elementary school teacher before turning her focus to the plight of farmworkers and teaming up with Chávez to create the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which became United Farm Workers.

Then president Barack Obama, who borrowed her rallying cry for his campaign slogan, “Yes we can,” awarded her with the nation’s highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, in 2012. Well into her 90s, Huerta was a familiar face at news conferences and rallies in Sacramento, where she advocated for the rights of workers, women, voters and others.
She revealed this year that she was sexually abused by Chávez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years.

Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The lawsuit seeks a court order directing OpenAI to stop violating the law, ensure its testing and development of its models are done safely and pay for its violations

items: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company of developing unsafe AI models that led to cyberattacks, including an incident involving the AI startup Hugging Face.
The lawsuit claims OpenAI violated California consumer protection laws and created a public nuisance, seeking a court order to enforce safer testing and development practices.
OpenAI is already facing multiple lawsuits from various states regarding the safety of its AI models, with increasing pressure on US legislators to regulate AI development and ensure accountability.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, November 16, accusing the company of developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks.

The lawsuit is the first filed by a state over the cyberattacks, which have drawn widespread attention since the revelation in July that an autonomous agents ​powered by OpenAI’s advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue during a security test and hacked ‌AI startup Hugging Face. Filed in state court in San Francisco, the lawsuit accuses the company of violating California consumer protection law and creating a public nuisance by risking public safety.
A representative for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit seeks a court order directing the company to stop violating the law, ensure its testing and development of its models are done safely and pay for its violations, Bonta, a Democrat, said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit.

“The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit accuses the company of misleading consumers about its efforts to test its models safely, in violation of the state’s consumer protection laws, and of impeding Californians’ use of property by disrupting local organizations and services.
After the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI said in a blog post that the breakout was “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.”

OpenAI acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the ​side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

OpenAI and other AI firms have disclosed a series of other AI agent breakouts, ​often weeks or months after they occurred, and in some cases only after independent researchers discovered them. The Trump administration and US legislators ​face mounting pressure to address the risk, particularly to the energy and banking sectors and emergency services.
US legislators are debating AI regulation, with some proposing a bill that would require developers of the most powerful ⁠AI models to ​submit them for independent security audits.
Multiple attorneys general have said they are investigating breaches tied to OpenAI’s models.

OpenAI is already facing several other states’ lawsuits over the safety of its models for users. Last month, a bipartisan group of eight states ​sued OpenAI in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT coached users, including teenagers, to harm themselves or others.

The company is also the subject of lawsuits filed by people who say they were harmed as a result of the chatbot’s actions, including more than 30 filed over a mass shooting that took place in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February. An OpenAI spokesperson called the shooting a tragedy and said the company has strengthened ChatGPT safeguards. – Rappler.com

articles.title: David Jones’ total debt is over $400m including millions owed to staff, administrators confirm
articles.summary:
Creditors meeting hears upmarket retailer owes $11m to employees and recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year

Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into administration earlier this…

blocks.text: Upmarket retailer David Jones collapsed into administration earlier this month owing well over $400m, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol broke down the 188-year-old chain’s massive debt pile, including an estimated $180m owed to suppliers and $11m to employees.

There is also about $33m in unredeemed gift cards held by shoppers, which the retailer is still accepting, and significant sums owed to secured creditors including the retailer’s main financier, Hilco.
David Jones collapsed into voluntary administration in early November after years of steep losses left the heritage retailer falling behind on rent and supplier payments.
The retailer is set to shutter half of its 38 department stores by the end of the year, triggering mass job losses under a sweeping restructure.
Under a dual appointment, FTI Consulting has day-to-day control of operations, while administrators McGrathNicol seek a buyer or fresh injection of capital.

David Jones recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, according to updated figures disclosed to creditors. It lost a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
Guardian Australia has reported that some suppliers are owed money from stock sent as early as April.

articles.title: Rio Tinto agrees to pay US$250m to begin repairing ‘devastation’ left by Panguna mine
articles.summary:
Bougainville cabinet minister says fund gives chance to find solutions to ‘huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation’

Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has…

blocks.text: Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto has agreed to pay a quarter-of-a-billion dollars to begin the clean-up of the toxic Panguna mine site it abandoned more than three decades ago.

Panguna, once one of the world’s most profitable gold and copper mines, was shuttered in 1989 after violent protests over environmental damage and the inequitable division of the mine’s profits sparked a decade-long civil war on the Papua New Guinean island of Bougainville.
But the sprawling mine pit, once a mountain, remains a scar in the middle of the island, with vast pillars of rubble at risk of collapse, and polluted rivers running bright blue with toxins.

Rio Tinto was forced from the island and has never returned, but in recent years has been part of a detailed consultation process with landowners and government. It has now agreed to voluntarily contribute US$250m (A$370m) towards the remediation of the mine site.
Theonila Roka Matbob, a Panguna community leader, said the fund was a vital contribution towards repairing the “devastation left by the Panguna mine”.

“We have a lot of work still ahead of us, but the establishment of this fund gives us the chance to find solutions to the huge problems we have been living with since the days of the mine’s operation.

“No amount of money will restore the damage caused to the environment in Panguna, but this sets a foundation for us to invest in addressing the environmental issues and invest in our children’s futures as well.”

blocks.caption: Bougainville minister Theonila Roka Matbob in her village of Mako ’Osi below the Panguna mine. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: Roka Matbob said the most fundamental remediation was to improve “accessibility” for the people living around Panguna – “accessibility to clean drinking water that is safe and secure … and infrastructure, in bridges that makes people’s access to trade, to school, to health[care], much easier. This is one critical area that immediately needs attention.”

The president of Bougainville, Ishmael Toroama, seeking to become the world’s newest head of state at the forefront of a long-running independence movement on the island, said the money would make a “meaningful difference” to villages and communities that had suffered from the impacts of the mine’s pollution.

“This work will deliver benefits not only for people today, but for future generations. Continued engagement with our communities will be essential to ensuring the work responds to local priorities and delivers lasting outcomes.”

The Rio commitment has emerged from the Panguna Mine Legacy Impact Assessment consultation process, which was initiated in response to a human rights complaint brought by the Australian-based Human Rights Law Centre, with Roka Matbob as the lead complainant.
Keren Adams, the HRLC’s legal director, said establishing the fund had taken years of work.
“It is a testament to the courage and persistence of community leaders, and the willingness of all parties to engage in difficult but constructive dialogue,” she said.
“The significant funding contributed by Rio Tinto creates a real opportunity to now address an environmental disaster that has remained unresolved for decades.”

Mark Davies, Rio Tinto’s chief safety and technical officer, said the establishment of the fund was an “important milestone … intended to support the transition from the assessment to practical remedy implementation”.
“Community engagement is an important next step to identify priorities and we remain committed to working with communities to shape the activities supported by the fund.”
The quarter-of-a-billion dollars will not be sufficient to entirely remediate the mine site, but it is being seen as a major step towards rehabilitation.
The funding commitment for Panguna comes at an acutely sensitive time for the restive Bougainville island.

The mine has become inextricably linked with the Bougainville’s political future: restarting operations at Panguna – believed to still hold at least $60bn in unrealised reserves – is seen by many, including the president, as the fundamental financial basis for the island’s independent future. Indian miner Lloyds has been granted a 25-year large-scale mining lease, but any future mining is years from starting.
What caused the Bougainville civil war?
Bougainville, a group of islands off Papua New Guinea to the north of Australia, has been variously controlled by Britain, Germany, Japan, Australia and PNG.
It declared independence in 1975 as the Republic of North Solomons, but was absorbed into the newly independent PNG weeks later.
Its close ethnic ties and proximity to the Solomons archipelago means it has always sat uneasily with Port Moresby’s rule.
That discontent came to a violent head in 1988 after a long-running dispute over the lucrative Panguna copper and gold mine.
The mine, carved from a mountain in central Bougainville, was critically important to PNG, at one point generating more than 45% of the country's national export revenue.

Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly US$2bn from the mine over 17 years of operation. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands had been destroyed by it.
Under the leadership of a former mine worker, Francis Ona, disaffected Bougainvilleans ran a sabotage campaign which forced the mine’s closure in 1989.

The PNG Government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war that ran for a decade, and saw as many as 20,000 people die.
PNG later hired international mercenaries to end the conflict (the notorious Sandline affair), before a peace agreement was signed in 2001.
In a 2019 referendum, 97.7% of Bougainvilleans voted in favour of independence. Many argue that reopening Panguna mine will be key to the island’s economic future as an independent nation.

Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it.

Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as “the crisis” – that ran for a decade. Between 15,000 and 20,000 people were killed, roughly 10% of the island’s population.

A recent environmental impact assessment found the abandoned mine remains an acute threat to people’s lives, including from landslides, levee collapses and floods. Untouched, the river delta will stay polluted for a century.

The future of Bougainville’s independence campaign is now before the PNG parliament, which will decide whether or not to recognise a UN-backed independence referendum held on the island in 2019, in which 97.7% of voters were in favour of Bougainville seceding and becoming an independent country.
The PNG parliament, which heard lengthy and impassioned debate over Bougainville last month, appears almost certain to vote against recognising the referendum result.

But Toroama, who has staked his presidency on achieving political independence, has said, regardless of the parliament’s decision, Bougainville will enter a period of “self-government” from September next year, before seceding, breaking away from PNG as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.

articles.title: Truck driver fired for ‘unsafe’ use of smartglasses in first reported sacking over device in Australia
articles.summary:
Toll employee Ricardo Martins Silva used smartglasses to take photos at an LPG terminal despite the risk of an explosion caused by an electrical spark, a court heard

  • Get our

blocks.text: A Toll truck driver was fired from work in Victoria after using smartglasses to snap photos at an LPG terminal, in what was described as an “intrinsically unsafe” incident.
It is the first reported case in Australia of a worker dismissed for using smartglasses in a workplace.

The employee, Ricardo Martins Silva, was fired from Toll Transport in July 2025, after eight months with the company as an LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) tanker driver, the federal circuit court heard. His role was to drive a loaded LPG tanker for Origin Energy from the Long Island Point terminal in Hastings, Victoria, for onward delivery.

A federal circuit court judgment last week stated that on 17 June 2025, Martins Silva raised concerns about a truck allocated to him, telling superiors the truck had too much vibration and was jumping excessively.

The judgment stated he was advised to take a different truck, and when he went to the terminal, he took photographs using his smartglasses, and sent them to a superior with a message stating: “I’m going to take the truck back to Dandenong and I’m leaving! There’s no more time for deliveries today!”
The Esso worker at the terminal told Toll that any use of electrical equipment on-site is “intrinsically unsafe” due to the risk of an explosion caused by electrical spark.

Martins Silva was prevented from taking on additional work until an investigation into the incident had been completed, and Origin Energy later asked the employee be removed from work as soon as possible because “his attitude is poor” and “not doing planned deliveries because he is ‘tired and stressed’ is not acceptable”, the judgment read.

Martins Silva sent emails between 17 and 19 June raising concerns about his role, truck allocations and safety issues. The worker on 20 June submitted a complaint about his employment, including safety, and impact of working conditions on his health, among other things.
On 22 June, the employee was advised he was stood down, the judgment stated.

At a meeting on 24 June, what Toll termed as “the glasses incident” was raised with the employee. He was told it was regarded as a “critical safety breach” and that Toll had commenced an investigation process due to its seriousness.

By 30 June, the company decided Martins Silva should be suspended from employment citing, among other reasons, the seriousness of the glasses incident. On 9 July, the employee was informed that taking a photograph with the smartglasses was in breach of Toll’s code of practice, and his contract of employment. His employment was terminated on 18 July, the judgment stated.
Martins Silva claimed the action was in breach of the Fair Work Act, arguing Toll’s actions were as a result of complaints he had made.
The federal circuit court found in the ruling last week that the glasses incident was “on any objective view a serious incident”.
after newsletter promotion

“On the day he wore the smart glasses, Mr Martins Silva was plainly aware of the risks of what he was doing – he went so far as to seek to mitigate the risk by covering his smartglasses with safety glasses,” the ruling from federal circuit justice Karl Blake stated.
“The glasses incident was not concocted or made to look more serious than what it was. It was objectively very serious.”

Martins Silva had conceded in cross examination that he knew at the time he had done the wrong thing, Blake’s judgment stated, but had written to his employer at the time that his judgment had been affected by the unresolved trauma of a truck fire in which he had been injured in March 2025.

Blake found Martins Silva was not dismissed because he made complaints but “because he wore smartglasses” at the terminal and his employer was of the view that it amounted to a serious safety incident. The application was dismissed.

While the case had focused on safety concerns, since the arrival of Meta’s Ray-Bans and cheaper alternatives such as the Kmart Anko brand glasses, governments have faced pressure to ban the devices over privacy concerns.
Councils across Australia have banned the glasses from some public spaces including gyms and pools, while the federal government is considering bans in government offices.

articles.title: Fiona the hippo under veterinary care after eating hat at Cincinnati zoo
articles.summary:
Knit hat caught in ceiling fan and flung into enclosure eaten by Fiona, who is being closely monitored by zoo staff

The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global…

blocks.text: The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure.
Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said. The zoo said she received fluids and an enema Sunday to help move things through her system.

The cap got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told Axios in a statement, emphasizing it was an accident. Fiona will be off the exhibit until she is in better health.
Fiona was born six weeks premature in January 2017, and her fight to survive grabbed international attention.
She initially could not stand on her own and weighed just 29lbs (13.2kg) at birth, 25lbs (11.3kg) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Fans followed her progress online, and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
One couple even got engaged in front of her exhibit, with Fiona getting into the picture while underwater in the background.

Other zoos contacted Fiona, showing concern for her health. Timothy, the hippo at the San Antonio zoo sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
The zoo said in a social media post it will share more information as they get it, also reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
“If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.

articles.title: Around 10K protesters expected to join rally vs Trump amid ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: Around 10,000 protesters are expected to join the rally against the visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 9:05am
Around 10,000 protesters are expected to join the rally against the visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit on Tuesday.

Protesters earlier gathered along Padre Burgos Avenue in Manila to oppose Trump's attendance at the summit and the Philippines' participation in the Pax Silica initiative, according to a report by GMA News’ Jun Veneracion on Unang Balita.
Clashes broke out between protesters and police near Liwasang Bonifacio, prompting the Manila Police District (MPD) to arrest 11 individuals, including a minor.
Some police officers were injured after allegedly being hit by objects thrown by protesters and being struck during the confrontation, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said.

“The PNP will enforce the law and will not abide any violation of it, especially during this time. Ito po 'yung mga nasugatan natin. Some suffered injuries to the head noong binato at pinagpapalo po sila,” PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said.

(The PNP will enforce the law and will not abide by any violation of it, especially during this time. These are the ones who were injured. Some suffered injuries to the head when they were stoned and beaten.)
MPD director Police Brigadier General Arnold Santiago reminded the protesters to observe the law and avoid actions that could lead to violations.

“Huwag kayong lalabas ng freedom park. Hindi namin pinagkakait. May mga batas tayong pinasusunod. Huwag tayo lalagpas doon sa sinasaad ng batas. Kapag lumagpas tayo doon, magkakaproblema tayo,” Santiago said.
(Don't leave the freedom park. We are not denying you. We have laws to follow. Let's not go beyond what the law says. If we go beyond that, we will have problems.)

Meanwhile, protest organizers said more participants from different regions were still traveling to Manila to join the demonstration. The protesters did not push through with their original plan to march toward the US Embassy.

“Kailangan pa muna hintayin 'yung iba pang delegasyon galing sa iba't ibang rehiyon na naglalakbay pa ngayon dahil in-interrupt nga. Humaharap tayo sa napakaraming iba't ibang forms of harassment ng PNP,” Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) chairperson Jerome Adonis said.
(We still have to wait for the other delegations from different regions who are still traveling because they were interrupted. We are facing so many different forms of harassment by the PNP.)
Protesters maintained that they would proceed with their planned march toward the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), where the ASEAN Summit is being held.
“Tingin namin mas dadami pa ito at talagang mahihirapan ang pulis na pigilan ang pagprotesta ng mamamayan,” Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) chairperson Teddy Casiño said.
(We think this will increase even more and it will be really difficult for the police to stop the people’s protests.)
BAYAN and other organizations are set to conduct the “Trump Out rally” on Tuesday at 2 p.m., where protesters are expected to march from Liwasang Bonifacio to PICC.—Joviland Rita/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Romualdez in jail: VIP treatment vs humanitarian aid
articles.summary: The former House speaker's VIP medical arrangements while in detention highlights a deeper, systemic crisis of custodial neglect and routine mortality among ordinary detainees

blocks.text: Another controversy has hit the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) regarding a humanitarian arrangement allowed for detained former House speaker Martin Romualdez at the Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory.

Allegations emerged that a personal assistant attended to his medical needs around the clock. The jail warden clarified to the Sandiganbayan that the assistant was on call rather than residing full-time in the facility, primarily providing medical assistance when needed.

More critically, the warden acknowledged that the jail lacks sufficient medical personnel to manage detainees’ health and mental health needs. Similar arrangements had been extended to other vulnerable persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) whose families could assist. Rather than being a unique perk for a politician, the practice evolved to offset systemic correctional shortfalls. However, this explanation triggered intense public pushback.

Critics decried preferential VIP treatment, alleging bribery and covert accommodations by the administration. Given that the President is the former speaker’s first cousin, suspicions arose that his detention was merely performative justice — punished in public while kept comfortable in private. While these serious claims warrant investigation, they must be separated from speculation as the public demands equal treatment across all detainees.

Beyond accountability for high-level corruption, this controversy highlights endearingly chronic deficiencies in custodial medical care. Framing the issue solely through a partisan lens risks obscuring the deeper, systemic crisis.

Lost in political debates is the dire reality of medical care in Philippine prisons, where thousands of ordinary detainees die quietly each year without public outrage or legislative inquiry. Most victims are impoverished individuals whose deaths go unnoticed by the public.

Recent statistics reveal that 522 PDLs died under BJMP custody as of September 2026, while the Bureau of Corrections recorded 1,030 deaths in its facilities. In 2025, combined deaths reached 1,996 across both systems — averaging more than five deaths every single day in institutions responsible for protecting detainee lives.

These routine fatalities represent a de facto death penalty inflicted through systemic neglect. For pre-trial detainees who are legally presumed innocent, severe confinement conditions violate fundamental constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

Severe congestion, inadequate medical staffing, poor sanitation, and meager budgets drive these high mortality rates. Facility overcrowding accelerates the transmission of communicable diseases, while chronic resource shortages leave serious conditions untreated until they become fatal.

To survive, detainees and staff rely on informal coping strategies. Families supply outside medications, while medically trained inmates assist infirmary staff. Wealthier families sometimes pay inmate caregivers or contribute to shared dormitory funds to cover basic health needs for destitute prisoners. Though unauthorized by formal rules, these practices are tacitly tolerated to prevent institutional collapse.

blocks.caption: Philippines only starting to probe ‘silent tragedy’ of prison deaths

blocks.text: However, reliance on informal arrangements creates wide disparities in care. Inmates with financial means or personal influence receive timely medical intervention, whereas impoverished detainees face severe neglect, fostering systemic favoritism and corruption.

Distinguishing between necessary humanitarian accommodation and corrupt favoritism is vital. While preserving life is a state duty, conditioning care on wealth or political standing degrades fundamental rights into privileges. Strictly enforcing rules without resolving resource shortages will only exacerbate inmate suffering.

Correctional administrators face a double bind: strictly enforcing inadequate rules risks detainee deaths and public outrage, while permitting external family assistance risks accusations of political favoritism and corruption. Investigations must distinguish illicit financial exchanges from reasonable efforts to prevent fatalities due to staffing shortages.

The judiciary and oversight bodies must address systemic deficiencies rather than singling out individual officers. Reducing overcrowding, expanding non-custodial options for low-risk or ill detainees, and standardizing medical access are essential steps to ensure correctional health measures depend on medical need rather than status.

Eliminating preferential treatment requires establishing a uniform, basic standard of care across all facilities. True equality in the justice system means expanding humane health protections for underprivileged detainees, ensuring that basic human rights are upheld for all persons in state custody. – Rappler.com
Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.
The author originally posted a longer version of this \to Facebook on November 11, 2026.

articles.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies about escape attempt during alleged kidnapping
articles.summary: Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described how he tried to escape and how his alleged kidnappers ultimately released him during his continued testimony at their jury trial in Toronto on…

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described how he tried to escape and how his alleged kidnappers ultimately released him during his continued testimony at their jury trial in Toronto on Monday.
Pleterski also recounted threats to his family, beating with golf clubs and his release
'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski testifies about alleged 3-day kidnapping ordeal
Pleterski, 27, testified that he was zip-tied and taped to a chair in a "run-down, old home" in the Niagara Region in Ontario on the third and final day of his alleged kidnapping in December 2022.

He also recounted having a COVID-19 mask duct-taped to his face, and more duct tape wrapped around his head and eyes, before he was left in the care of a couple he said told him they'd been paid $5,000 "in dope" to keep him there.
"'What if I can try and convince them I can give them money to let me go?'" Pleterski said in Ontario Superior Court, recounting his thinking at the time.
Pleterski testified this photo was taken of him while he was being held at a home in the Niagara Region during his alleged kidnapping December 2022. (Ontario Superior Court)

Pleterski testified he started telling the couple details from his bankruptcy proceeding, hoping they'd heard of his case, as well as the same "story" he'd told his alleged kidnappers about his former landlord, Sandeep Gupta, hiding money for him.

He said he offered to give the couple $50,000 to $100,000 to release him and would set them up in a hotel downtown Toronto for a few days. Pleterski told the court the couple agreed and rushed him out of the house.

But instead of leaving with them, Pleterski testified he was thrown back into the same Dodge Ram truck he'd been in and out of for three days with his alleged captors. Pleterski said they had a new plan to release him so he could get them money.
"Kid, you're going to go to Sandeep and you're going to get all your assets," Pleterski testified that someone identified as "Slime" told him.
"He said if I don't get money from Sandeep, he's going to kill my family."
"Slime" was the lead kidnapper, according to the Crown, but he is not part of this trial.

Two other men, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry, who Pleterski testified were also in the truck at that time and part of his kidnapping, are on trial for that and for allegedly extorting and assaulting him.

From left to right, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, Instagram/atlanticmastoronto, Evan Mitsui/CBC)

A third man, Akil Heywood, who allegedly invested more than $300,000 with Pleterski and lost a significant amount of it, is also accused of kidnapping and extortion. The Crown described him as the "driving force" behind the plan to kidnap Pleterski.
All three men have pleaded not guilty.
Pleterski was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf, but he has yet to be sentenced.
Released at the Ritz

During their drive back toward Toronto from the Niagara Region, Pleterski said Slime kept oscillating between the plan to let him go to get money from Gupta and giving Pleterski to other groups that wanted him.
"'If they were going to kill me, they would have done it, and if they kill me they won't get money out of me,'" said Pleterski about what he was thinking at the time.
"At this point I'm pleading with him to drop me off with Sandeep."
Pleterski demonstrates how he was grabbed by his alleged kidnappers during his testimony at their jury trial in Toronto last Friday. (Pam Davies/CBC)
Pleterski also testified that the truck stopped at a Walmart along the way. The jury was shown security footage of this.

At the big box store, Pleterski said Paladino purchased a SIM card, which was put in an old iPhone given to Pleterski with two numbers saved in it: one for "John Doe," to communicate with the alleged kidnappers, the other for Gupta.
From there, he said Slime "threw the phone at me" and told him "kid, if you don't do this, your family is going to get smoked."

items: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
Crypto King's alleged kidnappers’ trial hears call Aiden Pleterski made to landlord asking for $3M

blocks.text: Pleterski said Slime, Paladino and Henry dropped him off across the street from the Ritz-Carlton in downtown Toronto, where Gupta was living. More security footage was played in court of Pleterski outside the hotel that night.

He phoned Gupta, who he said told him "teams of police" were looking for him. Soon after an officer found him in the lobby of the hotel while Pleterski said he was on the phone with his father telling him he was OK.
Failed meeting

Earlier Monday, Pleterski also described how he was coached to set up a meeting with Gupta at a Tim Hortons in Toronto the previous day, but his alleged captors bailed on the meeting and started heading toward London, Ont.
"When [we] started going toward the highway, my heart sunk a little bit," said Pleterski. "When Slime said there were police there, I felt very scared of what they were going to do to me."
Gupta, testified about the same calls and attempted meeting last week during his own testimony as the Crown's first witness.
Sandeep Gupta, Pleterski's former landlord, testified last week at the trial of three men accused of kidnapping Pleterski. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski testified about how in London, he was allegedly hit in the face with a pistol and beaten with golf clubs after his alleged kidnappers learned someone he'd convinced them to call had contacted Pleterski's family trying to get money.
When they left the city, Pleterski said his alleged kidnappers appeared to follow a Dodge Durango to the Niagara Region, eventually stopping at the house where Pleterski later tried to escape.

While being led into the house, Pletersi testified that he recognized the voice of another man, who he said was present earlier in his kidnapping when he was forced to record a confession video in the basement of a home in the Pickering area, east of Toronto.
Pleterski is expected to continue his testimony Tuesday morning.

Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

items: US President Donald Trump is visiting Manila and Shenzhen for meetings with regional leaders and a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, amid heightened tensions following midterm election losses and allegations of a Chinese spy.
Trump may also meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his trip, although North Korea has shown no intention of engaging with the US at this time.

The upcoming discussions will focus on denuclearization, trade, and technology issues, with analysts suggesting that Trump's political vulnerabilities could influence the dynamics of US-China relations.

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump headed to Manila on Monday, November 16, after a midterm election drubbing and allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy that have raised the stakes for his latest meeting with Beijing’s powerful leader, Xi Jinping.
As he left the White House, Trump said he might also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise announcement that could reshape his swing through the region if it in fact occurs.

Trump will first visit Manila for meetings with Southeast Asian and other regional leaders on Tuesday before jetting to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where he will meet the Chinese president and hold three-way discussions with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

blocks.caption: Trump says he might meet with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un in China

blocks.text: Trump said he would discuss denuclearization, Iran and Ukraine in the meeting with Putin and Xi, as well as trade and the economy.
“We may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said, adding: “He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”

The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 term and has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting, but has also previewed meetings that never took place, including during a trip to Asia last year.
North Korea, whose mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has publicly indicated it has no intention of meeting with the US president at this time.

With a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China extended to early next year, and more Trump-Xi talks due in December at the G20 in Miami, some analysts had initially billed the Shenzhen meeting as a low-stakes summit.

But a backlash against Trump’s Republican Party in this month’s midterms and criticism that his administration failed to act on intelligence that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has close ties to Trump, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy have muddied those expectations.
Chinese analysts say there are concerns in China that allegations that restricted semiconductors were diverted to Chinese customers could harden US attitudes toward China.

“With less reason to worry about market reactions or electoral fallout, (Trump) may be more willing to consider disruptive measures,” said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser on China at the Tony Blair Institute, a London-based think tank.
Washington has already signaled such willingness ahead of the meeting, urging China to live up to its commitments made under the truce agreed between Trump and Xi a year ago.

And on Monday, the Trump administration issued a rule that will restrict chip exports to overseas data centers in countries like Malaysia and Thailand and hurt Chinese companies that use these to access advanced AI chips to train their artificial intelligence models.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson said last week there was growing consensus in Congress on further limiting Chinese access to advanced chips after the scandal, and Democrats are expected to press hard on the issue when they take over the House and Senate majorities in January.

Zhu Feng, director of the Institute of International Studies at Nanjing University, said the spat could also speed up “the decoupling of AI” between the world’s two superpowers even as they try to cooperate on mitigating the technology’s risks.

China has said the US has fabricated the spy narrative to justify a technological blockade. One senior US administration official said the Nvidia situation “should not really have any bearing on the trip,” on which analysts say Trump may want to focus on legacy-building.
Trump said on Monday he would not mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO and that he did not believe his relationship with the tech executive had put national security at risk.

Trump sees the unprecedented summit with Xi and Putin as possibly providing movement toward an agreement on nuclear arms control. But that is a non-starter for China, which has far fewer warheads than the others, Chinese analysts said.

The proposed three-way meeting has drawn comparisons, particularly in Russia, with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
Such a framing is particularly worrisome for Ukraine, which is engaged in a four-year war with Russia.
The Kremlin said on Monday that the meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi would have a major impact on global affairs.
Some analysts say Xi could seek to take advantage of Trump’s political weakness after his election humbling.

Top of Beijing’s wish list is ensuring the US president doesn’t approve a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, which China claims as its own. Trump has said he is holding the arms back as a “negotiating chip” with China.

“Xi just needs Trump to remain reluctant to revert toward a more competitive posture toward China for as long as possible,” said Jonathan Czin, a foreign policy analyst at the Brookings Institution, a US-based think tank, and a former director for China at the US National Security Council.

He said Beijing will be acutely aware that whoever succeeds Trump when his term ends in two years may be less accommodating and “will take whatever time it can get to fortify itself for the next round in the contest.”

Despite the frustration the US has voiced over Chinese implementation of the terms of a truce in a trade war that threatened the global economy last year, analysts like Kurt Tong, a former senior State Department official now with the Asia Group think tank, expect that deal to be further extended beyond its January 10 expiration.

“The two sides are quite incentivized to maintain this fragile stability … despite also having some disagreements,” said senior China analyst Chim Lee at the Economist Intelligence Unit. “They both have quite a lot to lose.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Volunteers back in Manitoba after grounding of U.S. flights set them on long road trip home
articles.summary: A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.

image.caption: Doug Brown, a former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player working for a health-care equipment company, was among a group of about 40 people who took a 28-hour bus trip on their way back from a volunteer journey to Central America. (Submitted by Doug Brown)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
A group of Manitobans doing volunteer work are back home after Friday's closure of U.S. airspace forced them on a long journey across that country.
28-hour bus trip anything but comfortable for about 40 returning from Nicaragua, including former Blue Bomber
Doug Brown was returning from Nicaragua with about 40 other volunteers with Operation Walk Manitoba, a charity that provides surgical treatments to people in developing countries.

The former Winnipeg Blue Bombers player works for a medical device company. He was aboard a flight from Managua to Houston, Texas, when he learned U.S. authorities had grounded flights nationwide, causing tens of thousands of flight cancellations over the weekend.
"We were literally just about an hour and a half out of Houston, and we all found out via the internet," Brown said Monday.
"I thought it was some sort of AI-fabricated joke."
The nationwide stop, the longest in 25 years, was in place for about four hours Friday.
U.S. officials said a contractor was replacing a copper wire with fibre optic cable when an unknown issue triggered an air traffic control system outage.
Brown's plane landed in Houston, but the outage delayed a connecting flight that would take the cohort of volunteers he was with to Denver.

items: Winnipeg film producer, family resume trip to L.A. after 24-hour delay in Minneapolis
Winnipeg airport asks passengers to check flight status amid U.S. stoppage

blocks.text: With cancellations rolling over into Saturday morning, the charity chartered a bus driving the volunteers back to Winnipeg instead.
The trip was about 28 hours long, Brown said.
"First stop, we went to Walmart just so we could get supplies," he said.
He bought pillows, a blanket, electrolyte water and a couple of apples.
Two Americans would alternate driving the bus, one taking over while the other slept.
"We didn't stop for dinner. We didn't stop overnight. We just essentially stopped when the bus needed fuel," Brown said.
"When we finally got to Winnipeg…, I almost laid down on the ground," he said.
"We hadn't showered or whatever in 24 hours. I was able to brush my teeth twice, but [it was the] first time I've done that at truck stops, right?…. It was a different world."
Sense of perspective

A team of nearly 70 volunteers was in Nicaragua for more than a week as part of the mission, with medical professionals performing hip replacement surgery to patients with severe joint disease who can't access that kind of care in the Central American country.
Medical lead Eric Bohm was in a cohort that managed to avoid disruptions while getting back to Manitoba.
Eric Bohm welcomed the volunteers who were left stranded in Texas after the U.S. ground stop. (Submitted by Doug Brown)
Bohm said those who made it home as planned wanted to make the other volunteers feel special. He was there to receive them at the end of their trip in Winnipeg.
"I thought … these guys are going to be tired and hungry and a little bit bummed out," Bohm said.
"Let's try to welcome them back home with some posters and some people showing up and some gift bags.… Just remind them, you know, how much the people in Nicaragua appreciate what they're doing."

items: Canada-wide flight grounding unlikely, says aviation expert

blocks.text: Brown said he used to take a bus with the Bombers to Regina for the Labour Day Classic, but those trips were only about a quarter of the length of the 28-hour journey over the weekend.
He said nobody wanted anyone else to be in charge of the music. Everyone also wanted to avoid using the one tiny bathroom that was available.
At six feet eight inches tall, sitting in the bus was uncomfortable enough for the former professional athlete.
But Brown said the trip to Nicaragua gave him a sense of perspective.
"One of the surgeons on the bus ride said, you know, Nicaragua was one of the poorest nations in the entire Western Hemisphere.…
"This is still nothing compared to what the vast majority of those people go through on a daily basis."
Senior officials in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration blamed the grounding on aging air traffic control infrastructure and Congress underfunding.
With files from Meaghan Ketcheson

articles.title: Meta would 'consider' pulling services from Canada if lawful access bill passes as is
articles.summary: Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.

image.caption: Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp. (Richard Drew/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Updated
Representatives from Meta say the social media company would have to "consider" pulling encryption services from Canada if the government's proposed lawful access bill passes without further changes.
Company says government amendments don't protect encrypted data
Bill C-22 would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant.

The legislation is currently being studied in the Senate, where Meta representatives said the bill leaves encrypted information — meant only to be viewed by users sharing the information — vulnerable to malicious actors.

"Ultimately, the Canadian government would be enforcing and imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians," Robyn Greene, Meta's director of privacy and public policy, told senators on the national security committee on Monday evening.
Meta services include Facebook, Instagram and the encrypted messaging app WhatsApp.

When asked if the legislation would mean the company would pull some of its services from Canada, Meta's head of public policy for Canada Rachel Curran said the company would have to "review all of our options."
But she said it is something the company would have to "consider."
Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree proposed amendments to the lawful access legislation, but critics say they don't go far enough. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Bill C-22 also grants the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers (ESPs) operating in Canada, requiring them to build surveillance and monitoring capabilities into their systems. Orders would first be reviewed by the intelligence commissioner — an independent quasi-judicial official.
Before the bill was sent to the Senate in June, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments that put limits on when companies would be required to decrypt information.

Another change reduces the length of time that tech companies would have to retain metadata to six months from up to a year, after cybersecurity experts warned that data would be an attractive target for hackers.

items: Privacy watchdog urges Senate to further amend Bill C-22
Liberals to amend police data interception bill following searing criticism

blocks.text: Curran told the Senate committee that the government's amendments don't go far enough to protect encrypted data.
"They have protected just the core and not the outside layers that are an integral part of the encryption process," she said.
Encrypted messaging service Signal has also consistently said it would withdraw from Canada if the bill passes.
"If we are forced to choose between betraying our users and leaving Canada, we will not compromise the security of Canadians," Signal vice-president Udbhav Tiwari told the Senate committee.
Tiwari called on the government to make further changes to the bill, including explicit assurances to protect encrypted data.
Tech giant Apple also said earlier this month that the amendments aren't enough.

"While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple's ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses," the company said in a statement.
Privacy watchdog calls for changes

The government has argued that the bill is needed to ensure law enforcement has the legal tools to prevent, investigate and respond to modern crime and protect Canadians. Still, the proposed legislation has faced consistent pushback and this is the second lawful access bill the government has introduced this session.
Earlier this month, Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne urged the Senate committee to further amend the legislation to better protect the privacy of Canadians.

The bill would lower the legal threshold for law enforcement and intelligence bodies to access basic subscriber information — like names, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and account numbers — from "reasonable grounds to believe" down to "reasonable grounds to suspect" that an offence has been or will be committed.
Dufresne said the definition of subscriber information and who can be asked to hand it over remain overly broad relative to the lowered threshold required to access it.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Catharine Tunney and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Proposed NSW laws to allow coalmine to increase production pose ‘serious corruption risk’
articles.summary:
Bill to authorise expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, will be debated this week

  • Get our

blocks.text: A New South Wales government bill to increase coal production at a Hunter Valley coalmine creates a “serious corruption risk” for the state due to a clause that would give the resources minister “king-like” powers, the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson says.
The state parliament will this week debate legislation to allow MACH Energy to increase coal production at the Mount Pleasant mine in Muswellbrook by 32% to 16.5m tonnes per year.

The Minns government announced the bill last month after the high court ruled that an expansion of the mine was invalidly approved. The government has said the legislation is necessary to prevent 400 job losses at the site before Christmas.

Watson, the Greens and some members of the crossbench have raised concerns that a clause in the bill would give the resources minister of the day “unusually broad” powers to override other state laws.
Known as a Henry VIII clause, it would allow the minister to make regulations that could modify laws of the state as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development.
Henry VIII provisions are sometimes used by parliaments and draw their name from King Henry VIII and his style of governing by royal proclamation.
Watson is a director of the Centre for Public Integrity and Grata Fund and a former counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac).

In a legal analysis of the bill, he raised concerns that clause 17 “explicitly places” wide powers to “make new laws (or to repeal or modify existing laws) in the hands of one person – the mining minister – and for a single coalmine owner”.
“There are real problems with this as it is known that the concentration of this kind of power in the hands of one person creates a serious corruption risk,” he wrote.

blocks.caption: Geoffrey Watson says that corruption can include ‘undue influence’ and ‘decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest’. Photograph: Dan Peled/AAP

blocks.text: He said the risk was “heightened” because the Mount Pleasant bill had been created for a single private company. He wrote that while he imputed “no bad faith at all to the current mining minister”, past experience in the state “has shown that not all ministers have acted in a manner free from improper motives”.
“Historically, we’ve seen this concentration of power into the hands of a single decision maker as posing a serious risk of corruption,” Watson told Guardian Australia.
“Now, corruption in that sense may not mean money passing hands. It also includes undue influence, decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest.”

Elaine Johnson is the director of Johnson Legal, which represented the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg) in the high court proceedings. In a separate legal opinion, she raised similar concerns there was “a very obvious corruption risk arising from clause 17”.

She wrote that the clause gave the resources minister of the day “unfettered power to make regulations to change the application of any law of the state” to the mine, and said it could potentially affect many laws that applied to the mine, such as those that regulate noise and dust or worker safety.

A spokesperson for the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, said the purpose of the bill was to protect all permanent workers at Mount Pleasant and the government welcomed “constructive engagement” from crossbenchers.

The police minister and member for the Hunter Yasmin Catley, who will introduce the bill in the lower house, said on Tuesday morning the government had taken advice on the Henry VIII clause “and we believe that it’s sound”.

The lower house is expected to debate the legislation on Tuesday, followed by the upper house later this week. The Minns government is hoping to pass the bill in what is likely to be the final sitting week before the March 2027 election.
Both Labor and Coalition lower house seats are under pressure from One Nation in the Hunter, where the mine is located.
One Nation’s NSW leader and candidate for Cessnock, Mike Newman, has described the Minns government’s bill to increase production limits at Mount Pleasant as a “Band-Aid on a bullet wound”.
after newsletter promotion

The Coalition resources spokesperson and Nationals MP for Upper Hunter, Dave Layzell, said the opposition would not oppose Labor’s legislation “in any way”. Asked about the Henry VIII clause, he said the Coalition would follow advice on the bill from the parliament’s legislation review committee, which is expected on Tuesday.
“We recognise [Labor’s] argument about the need to protect the number of jobs they are quoting.
“We agree that it is important that we fix the situation with the Mount Pleasant Mine extension.
“We cannot allow green environmental lawfare to continue to delay projects that have the support of the majority of the community, and are approved on a technical basis by the planning system.”

blocks.caption: A protest in Sydney this month opposing the expansion of the Mount Pleasant coalmine. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Greens’ climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, said it was “the broadest” Henry VIII clause she had seen during the current parliament and the party would seek to remove it from the bill or limit its scope.
“Placing that much power in the hands of a single minister is a corruption risk the Labor government should know well,” she said.

“A tightly limited Henry VIII provision can be necessary to give effect to parliament’s decision over time, as with the recent Great Koala national park bill, where it allowed more land to be permanently protected in the public interest as it becomes available.”
The government spokesperson said the bill had been presented transparently to parliament.
“We welcome constructive engagement on the bill from crossbenchers and will engage with good-faith amendments as we always do,” they said.
“Any proposed regulation would be submitted to the executive council for approval and published transparently in the usual manner, and also subject to disallowance in the usual manner.”
They added that Henry VIII provisions had been “routinely” used in legislation for decades, including in bills the Greens had supported in this term of parliament.
The independent MP Alex Greenwich, who intends to oppose the bill as a whole, said the provision was “dangerously broad and quite unprecedented”.
“It’s especially concerning, given parliament won’t sit for six months, meaning regulations issued during that time won’t be able to be disallowed,” he said.

articles.title: Trump says he might meet with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un in China
articles.summary: Trump says while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader's presence was ultimately up to Chinese…

Trump says while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader's presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping

items: US President Donald Trump announced a potential meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, which could impact his East Asia trip.
Trump's previous attempts at diplomacy with Kim during his first term did not lead to denuclearization, and North Korea currently sees no need for talks.
The meeting's feasibility depends on Chinese President Xi Jinping, with analysts suggesting it could enhance Xi's diplomatic standing if it occurs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump said on Monday, November 16, he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China this week, an announcement that could dramatically reshape his trip through East Asia.
The president met the North Korean leader several times during his 2017-2021 first term in unprecedented direct diplomacy that failed to persuade Kim to give up his nuclear weapons.
Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in another meeting during his current term, but also previously previewed meetings with Kim that never took place, including during a trip to Asia last year.
Senior US officials have previously said he has no immediate plans for another meeting, while North Korea has said it sees no need for talks at this time and denounced hostile US policies.

Trump told reporters while departing the White House en route to the Philippines and China that any meeting would occur in China, and that the North Korean leader’s presence was ultimately up to Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“(Xi) was here … and we’re also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.
“So that’ll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.”
Trump added in reference to Kim: “He may come. I don’t know. That’s up to President Xi.”
North Korea’s mission to the United Nations did not respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.

The Kremlin said on Monday a planned meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi on the sidelines of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in China would have a major impact on global affairs.

Trump said he would discuss denuclearization, Iran and Ukraine with Xi and Putin, as well as trade and the economy, but US officials and analysts have played down the possibility of a meaningful agreement emerging.
Russia’s Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying later on Monday that Putin could meet Kim if he comes to China.

North Korea has sent about 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington’s Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, said Trump’s comments made clear he had asked Xi to bring Kim to China for a meeting.
“One could see a huge diplomatic victory for Kim if he were to share a stage with the US, Russia, China … the three other nuclear powers in Asia – in addition to any bilateral with Trump,” he said.

“The common narrative is that China would not want to distract from their hosting APEC but I think Xi’s global diplomacy offensive would probably be enhanced, in his mind, if he were bringing together all of the leaders for this extraordinary meeting,” Cha said.

Trump’s interest in renewed engagement with Kim comes seven years after their last summit ended without agreement when they failed to bridge differences over North Korea’s nuclear weapons and sanctions relief.

Since then, North Korea has significantly expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities while strengthening ties with Russia and China, and any willingness by Trump to make major concessions to Pyongyang risks creating friction with regional allies.

Trump has referred to North Korea as a nuclear power, a status allies in the region and the West have refused to recognize despite the dozens of nuclear warheads experts believe Pyongyang has built. – Rappler.com
