articles.title: PH hosts Melania Trump's global coalition for children's online safety, technology education
articles.summary: First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos hosted on Monday the initiative for children's safety and empowerment, which was led by United States First Lady Melania Trump, on the sidelines of the 49th Association…

blocks.text: Published November 17, 2026 7:51am

First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos hosted on Monday the initiative for children's safety and empowerment, which was led by United States First Lady Melanie Trump, on the sidelines of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

"Fostering the Future Together" is a global Coalition of First Spouses and equivalent leaders committed to helping children learn, grow, and thrive through safe and innovative use of advanced technology, including artificial intelligence.
During her speech in Pasay City, Araneta-Marcos said as technology opens opportunities, it also brings danger to children.
These dangers include cyberbullying, online exploitation, harmful content, and those taking advantage of children's innocence.

"We want our children to enjoy everything technology has to offer, but we also want them to be safe. And we certainly cannot expect them to navigate this complicated digital world all on their own," Araneta-Marcos said.
She added that the program has four pillars: artificial intelligence in education, education technology tools, online protection, and digital skills.

"The digital world, as you know, knows no borders, neither do the dangers that our children face. So I hope that today's conversation leads not only to the exchange of ideas, but to real partnerships and practical solutions that you can bring home to our respective communities and countries," Araneta-Marcos said.
Equip the next generation
In a video message, Melania Trump said the coalition aims to provide children tools to power the world's economy.

"Together, we can equip the next generation with the tools to power the world's economy (at scale) so that children in every corner of the planet can access and collaborate for prosperity, tolerance, and growth," Melanie Trump said.
"Let's leverage technology strategically so that every child's dream will be realized," she added.
Meanwhile, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton said strong partnership is needed to ensure technologies are applied for the betterment of humanity, especially the children.
"This is an international cooperation for our kids, their educations, their safety, their future, and the kind of world we want to be leaving them," Lipton said in his speech.
Under the initiative, participating technology companies have committed to provide students all over the world with tools to adopt to emerging technologies.
As of 2026, the initiative has 57 participating countries, including France, Poland, UAE, Panama, Philippines, Israel, Morocco, and Turkiye. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
articles.summary: Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.

image.caption: Flying high — Florian Wirtz and his teammates schooled neighbor and rival the Netherlands at Berlin Olympic Stadium in Monday's Nations League quarterfinalsImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.
It was the team's sixth game underhead coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game,attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."
Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.
Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.
By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who hascome under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025,and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

articles.title: Data centres in the U.S. put out more carbon emissions in a year than Denmark, says Harvard study
articles.summary: The 400 largest data centres in the United States put more heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence…

image.caption: In this aerial photo, an Amazon data centre is under construction Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in New Florence, Mo. A new study estimates that the massive electricity demands of hyperscale data centres in the U.S., combined with the fact that more than half of their electricity is generated through fossil

blocks.text: The 400 largest data centres in the United States put more heat-trapping gases into the atmosphere in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday.
Researchers found that more than half of the electricity powering hyperscale data centres in the U.S. was generated using fossil fuels, contributing to a significant increase in emissions.

The study results come as negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, which the U.S. skipped this year, launched a voluntary pledge Monday calling on companies and countries to power the world's data centres with clean energy and be more transparent about their power and water consumption and emissions.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."
As public opposition to data centres continues to mount, the political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites.

In Canada, plans for massive data centres have triggered protests in communities across the country, including this fall over a proposed data centre for AI giant Anthropic in Nova Scotia and a $52-billion data centre near Regina, Saskatchewan.
Inside the climate toll of data centres

Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centres between May 2024 and April 2025, using available data and modelling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity used by the centres produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to the study in Monday's Nature Sustainability.
The Dave Johnson coal-fired power plant is silhouetted against the morning sun in Glenrock, Wyo. in this 2018 file photo. (J. David Ake/ The Associated Press)

More than half their 82 terawatt-hours of electricity use, enough to power nearly seven million homes for a year, came from fossil fuels, the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. Coal, widely considered the most environmentally damaging fossil fuel, generated 15 per cent of the electricity used.

items: Protests across Nova Scotia oppose AI data centres
Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered

blocks.text: The emissions estimate is two to three times higher than previous studies had shown, said Francesca Dominici, the study's senior author and a Harvard biostatistics professor.
Big emitters 'profiting' from the planet's destruction: UN chief

"It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centres make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions."

items: Canada presented itself as a global leader in methane reductions at COP31. But is Alberta holding it back?
Why data centre communities worry about water
Bell AI data centre expansion raises questions over power, water and local impact

blocks.text: Researchers noted that data centre construction has only expanded since the study period, meaning emissions from this industry are probably even higher now.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," lead author Gianluca Guidi, postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics, said in a press release.
Nova Scotians rally against planned $10B AI facility

Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study reached realistic conclusions and that its use of modelling was reasonable because companies disclose little about their power consumption and pollution.

"We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't involved in the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centres, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity."
'Selling us hope while hiding the harms'

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, launched by COP31 host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centres should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems.
Canada's new data centre guidelines lack teeth, critics say

The pledge says the environmental impacts of data centres should be assessed and disclosed, but it also calls for harnessing artificial intelligence to help address climate change, which some climate experts see as a contradiction given AI's growing environmental footprint.

items: 'The planet is not dying, it is being killed' - Thunberg at COP 31
Canada can't control climate change on its own, economist tells landmark trial
Canada's credibility on the line at COP31 as it defends fossil fuel expansion while trumpeting clean energy

blocks.text: The explosion of new and planned data centres has driven demand for new sources of power generation and contributed to some of the biggest tech companies missing their climate goals, according to a report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation.

The report, published earlier this month, found that electricity consumption by Amazon, Microsoft and Google had risen 240 per cent between 2022 and 2025 amid the AI race. Its authors accused Big Tech of "greenwashing" AI by obscuring its current environmental impact behind claims of future climate gains.
Can AI save the planet before it wrecks it

Former U.S. vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said that while it is essential for data centres to be powered by carbon-free energy, he is hopeful their computing power could help find new ways to fight climate change.

items: AI is increasingly being used to deal with climate change, but it has its own emissions problem

blocks.text: In an interview with The Associated Press, Gore cited research by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern, who predicted that by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9 per cent reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy."

Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centres face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centres, but the fears may be overblown."
But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical.
"We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other," Newell said. "They're selling us hope while hiding the harms from us."

articles.title: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
articles.summary:
Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans

United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread…

blocks.text: United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.

The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.
The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.

And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.

Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

articles.title: Father calls for apology after son target of racist taunts at Kitchener, Ont., hockey tournament
articles.summary: The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener,…

image.caption: Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers and his dad Aaron Doxtator at Little NHL. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

blocks.text: Indigenous

The father of a 16-year-old hockey player says he wants a public apology and cultural-competency training for the league after his son was the target of racist taunts at a tournament in Kitchener, Ont., on Nov. 8.
Kitchener Minor Hockey Association and ALLIANCE Hockey investigating
In a video provided to CBC Indigenous, a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers can be heard telling Brantford 99ers player Ryder Doxtator "Go back to the rez."

Aaron Doxtator, Ryder's father, from Oneida Nation of the Thames, was at his son's game Nov. 8. He said his son told him that he'd also been called a "dirty Indian" by the same player. Although Aaron Doxtator said he was unable to hear it from the stands, he said other players and staff on Ryder's team and parents told him they also heard the slur.
As a former athlete in hockey and lacrosse who experienced this type of racism throughout his playing career, Aaron Doxtator said he can't believe it's still happening.
Ryder Doxtator of the Brantford 99ers was told to 'go back to the rez' by a player on the Kitchener Jr. Rangers. (Submitted by Aaron Doxtator)

"It's always the same words, 'Go back to where you came from. Go back to the rez, you dirty Indian, or go back to your teepees.' Those are all different words I've heard growing up … My older son, happened to him all the way up," Aaron Doxtator said.
"You just get a gross feeling in your stomach when you hear those words."
He said despite being proud of his home, "They're making you feel like you're lower, 'Get out of here. You know you don't belong here.'"

Doxtator said there was a brawl just after Ryder scored a goal with one minute left in the game. The referees broke it up and Ryder was put in the penalty box along with two teammates and three Kitchener Jr. Rangers players.
Doxtator said they were arguing back and forth and a Brantford 99ers trainer went over to the box "to try to defuse the situation and tell our player to calm down."
He said she and a couple of the other parents heard the Kitchener players saying 'go back to the rez' and 'go back to where you came from.'
He was told by officials that the video was under review.
Doxtator said this isn't the first time his son's dealt with racist taunts from opponents.
"It angered him because he's heard that before and it's discriminatory … We should be equal with people," he said.
He said he's lodged formal complaints with leagues before, but they just get "brushed under the rug" and "nothing comes of it."
2 pending investigations into incident
The Kitchener Minor Hockey Association (KMHA) said it received several emails regarding the incident and there are two investigations looking into the incident.

Roland Cyr, general manager for KMHA, said in an emailed statement to CBC Indigenous that KMHA "is aware of allegations involving the use of a racial slur during a game conducted under the jurisdiction of the association."

The statement continued that KMHA is also aware that the matter was reported to the on-ice officials during the game, who documented the allegations and submitted the report to the Minor Hockey Alliance of Ontario (ALLIANCE Hockey) for review.
The statement said KMHA takes the allegations seriously "and is committed to ensuring a safe, respectful, and inclusive environment for all participants in our sport."
It said in accordance with its policies, KMHA will be undertaking a review of the incident and ALLIANCE Hockey, the governing body for both teams, will conduct its own investigation.
Brantford 99ers general manager Kevin Murray declined to comment as the investigation is ongoing.
ALLIANCE Hockey said in an emailed statement it is aware “of an alleged incident that occurred on Nov. 8 at the Kitchener Blueline Tournament" and is taking it seriously.
Previously in 2022, one of KMHA's U-13 Kitchener Lady Rangers players used a racial slur against an opponent and the team had to issue an apology and take part in diversity training.
Racial slurs pop out as they're 'still part of their lexicon,' says academic
Janelle Joseph, Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University in St. Catharines, Ont., said incidents like this are sad but not surprising.
Joseph said there's been a lot of work around racial and gender justice in hockey which "continues to be run predominantly by that white majority."
"We are in the midst of a culture shift, but we're not on the other side of it," she said.
Joseph said players understand there are phrases they shouldn't say, "but if it's still part of their lexicon … when they get into the heat of a conflict, it spurts out."

Janelle Joseph is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Racial Justice, Health and Sport at Brock University and associate professor. She's also the founder and director of Canada's first research laboratory devoted to issues of race and movement cultures, the Indigeneity, Diaspora, Equity and Anti-racism in Sport (IDEAS) Research Lab. (Submitted by Janelle Joseph)

"That means that it was just always there. They were learning ways to cover it up or ways to communicate that would be more socially acceptable. But the anti-Indigenous racism, anti-Black racism, anti-immigrant and xenophobia is underlying in many, many of our communities."
Beyond superficial anti-racism training, Joseph said all teams would benefit from open dialogue about history and "what those expressions mean."
"When someone says 'go back to the rez,' what are they really saying there?" she said.
"I think we need to surface those kinds of conversations across every locker room, every team, so that we can start to make racism not something that happens over there, with those other people."
She said then we can start to see how some of those ideologies and understandings about who belongs and who doesn't are part of the dominant culture.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Candace Maracle is Kanien'kehá:ka, Wolf Clan from Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory. She has a master’s degree in journalism from Toronto Metropolitan University. Her latest short film, Tsi ní:yoht yonkwayentá:’on ne óhses (How We Got Maple Syrup) is completely in the Kanien’kéha language.

blocks.text: The federal government is backpedaling on its plan to cut backpacker numbers following criticism from regional stakeholder groups who rely on the travellers for labour.
The Albanese government is expected on Tuesday to lift the proposed cap on third-year working holiday visas, boost regional work requirements and delay the start of a new ballot system.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, previously announced in September plans to cap the number of third year backpackers to 5,000 from the current level of about 31,000.
Industry sources said they expected the government to back down and instead set a cap at 25,000 places.
Burke was due to hold a press conference in Cairns on Tuesday morning.

The home affairs minister announced major reforms to working holiday visas in September including creating a ballot for backpackers seeking to stay a second or third year which would require them to work in the regions.

Under that proposal, just 45,000 backpackers would be allowed to remain for a second year and would be required to work at least three months in a regional area, and just 5,000 places would be allocated for workers seeking to remain in Australia for a third year.
Industry sources expected second year backpackers will be required to work in regional areas for four months, instead of three, and that the ballot will be delayed.
The changes follow months of consultation with industry, regional and agricultural groups who warned of worker shortages under the crackdown.

Workers from the UK are exempt from the caps under the free trade agreement signed in 2021. Sources says the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is in discussions with his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, to force British backpackers to also do regional work going forward.

articles.title: The U.K. is granting pardons to women for past abortion convictions
articles.summary: The U.K. government says it will grant automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.

image.caption: Pro-choice protesters gather near U.K. Parliament during a vote to decriminalize abortion in June 2025. (Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New
The U.K. government says it will grant automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.
'Today is a historic day,' says a friend of a woman charged in 2020
The U.K. government is granting automatic pardons to all women convicted of having illegal abortions over the last 165 years.

What's more, it says it will expunge the records of those who have been investigated for abortion offences related to their own pregnancies, regardless of whether they were ultimately arrested or charged.

U.K. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who successfully fought to decriminalize abortion last year, says these clean records will bring justice to women who were "dragged from hospital beds to police cells."

"This trauma cannot be erased," Antoniazzi said. "I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to."
It started with decriminalization
The U.K.'s Abortion Act of 1967 allows legal abortions up to 24 weeks, under a specific set of criteria agreed upon by two doctors.

Until last year, women in England and Wales could be charged for procuring abortions outside that framework under a Victorian-era abortion ban, which is still on the books and carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

But in April 2025, U.K. Parliament voted to amend its Crime and Policing Bill so that people could not be prosecuted for "an abortion offence relating to their own pregnancy." It recieved royal assent in April of this year, and those amendments came into force on Monday.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.
But advocates cited what they described as an alarming increase in women being investigated for abortion-related offences, including several high-profile cases.

Nicola Packer, left, and her friend Helle Tumbridge. Packer was criminally charged in 2020 after she took legally prescribed abortion pills at home, not realizing she was past the legal threshold of 24 weeks. (Submitted by Helle Tumbridge)
Among them was Nicola Packer, who was criminally charged after she took legally prescribed abortion pills during the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020.
Packer, who argued she didn't know she was past the 24-week threshold for legal abortion, was cleared in a jury trial last year.
"It's a bittersweet day for her," Packer's friend and spokesperson, Helle Tumbridge, told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.
"She is, of course, pleased that this has happened … but, for her, this really never should have happened in the first place. And she will live with the trauma for the rest of her life."
LISTEN | Interview with Helle Tumbridge:
As It Happens6:36U.K. grants pardons to women convicted of having abortions. One advocate calls it a 'historic,' but 'bittersweet day'
Tumbridge says Packer experienced what's known as a cryptic pregnancy, which means that she didn't experience the tell-tale signs she was expecting.

As a result, she believed she was only a few weeks pregnant when she procured an over-the-phone prescription for mifepristone and misoprostol. It turned out, however, that she was 26 weeks pregnant, and the medication induced a stillbirth.
She required emergency surgery in hospital and, when she awoke, two police officers were waiting for her in the recovery room.
"Then, when she'd barely recovered, they took her off to the police station, where she was subjected to questioning and appalling treatment for a length of time," Tumbridge said.
"It took five years for her case to come to trial, so she was living all that time with this horrible trauma and stress, her life was on hold. And it was incredibly hard."
Tumbridge says her friend suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder and has authorized her to act as her voice in media interviews so she doesn't have to relive her experiences.
"While today is a historic day, it's an amazing day, and all campaigners and women everywhere are celebrating, I think for Nicola and the women involved, it is also a very difficult day," she said.
Doctors and abortion providers hail decision
The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) welcomed the decision in a joint letter with several reproductive rights organizations.

"Today's pardons are an important next step," said Dr. Alison Wright, RCOG's president. "They recognize the injustice of historical convictions and mean women no longer have to live with the consequences of a criminal record for something that should never have been treated as a crime."
The British Pregnancy Advisory Service, a U.K. charity and abortion provider, also welcomed the news.
"For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, the organization's chief executive.

The Society for the Protection of Unborn Children (SPUC), a U.K. anti-abortion group that opposed decriminalization, called the pardons an attempt to impose a "barbaric ideology on a past that showed more respect for human life."
In a written statement, SPUC spokesperson Alithea Williams decried the measure as "performative virtue signalling."
The Society for the Protection of Unborn Children organized a rally against the U.K.'s decriminalization measure in March 2026. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
The government has not said how many women will receive pardons or have their records cleared.
But Antoniazzi estimates that more than 100 women were investigated for abortion-related offences in the five years preceding last year's decriminalization vote.
According to the Guardian newspaper, those investigations include women, and at least one teenager, who were later determined to have had natural stillbirths and miscarriages.

Tumbridge, meanwhile, says Packer is calling for an official apology from the government, the police and the Crown Prosecution Service.
"We've had women doing jail time. It's really shocking," she said. "These cases should never have been brought to trial."

articles.title: Baby sea turtles swim out to sea after historic California nesting
articles.summary:
Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have…

blocks.text: Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”

A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”

blocks.caption: Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings are released in Huntington Beach, California. Photograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific

blocks.text: In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.

On September 16, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.

“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.

“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with, the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”

As Hurricane Polo began to form in late September, researchers with the aquarium and its federal and local partners relocated the 204 eggs from the two nests to incubate in the safety of the aquarium’s animal care facility.

“As animals adapt in unexpected ways to changes in their natural world, humans will need to adapt and make space to ensure endangered and threatened species are given a fighting chance,” said Jeff Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific.

“If they successfully hatch, these baby turtles will likely one day return to nest to carry on future generations on these very same beaches, giving us a remarkable opportunity to help a species expand its range and thrive.”

Even as the Huntington Beach and Seal Beach turtles have begun hatching and returned to the ocean, researchers are continuing to advise the public to be on the lookout for more nests. On 1 November, a third nest was recorded in Ventura county although those eggs were swept away by unusually high tides – likely also caused by El Niño.

articles.title: Military's No. 2 defends GlobalEye surveillance jets despite capability concerns
articles.summary: Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs…

image.caption: Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee is seen at a conference in Ottawa in March. He told MPs on Monday that he's satisfied with the program to purchase Saab's GlobalEye. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs he's satisfied with the procurement process, arguing the aircraft will contribute to an integrated continental defence network alongside satellites and ground-based radar systems.
Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee tells committee he's satisfied with program
The second in command of the Canadian military told parliamentarians on Monday that he's satisfied with the way the program to buy airborne early warning planes is unfolding.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee made the comments in testimony before the House of Commons defence committee, which is studying Bill C-40, legislation intended to turn the Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised many in the defence community by announcing Canada opened negotiations with Swedish defence giant Saab to purchase six of their GlobalEye surveillance jets — aircraft that would be militarized in Canada based upon a Bombardier 6500 airframe.
The federal government and the company have since agreed on a term sheet, a non-binding document that sets the stage for an eventual contract.

items: Feds sign preliminary deal with Saab for 6 GlobalEye aircraft
Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs

blocks.text: In early September, multiple sources told CBC News that the air force was concerned the GlobalEye meets only a handful of the military's requirements.

On Monday, federal Conservatives pressed Topshee, the vice-chief of the defence staff, for assurances that military requirements would not be sacrificed for the sake of building up the country's defence industrial base.
"I am comfortable with the path we're proceeding down," Topshee told the three-party committee, referring to the GlobalEye program.

He said the airborne surveillance capability is crucial for the defence of North America and ties into an integrated air and missile defence system with the United States — a program U.S. President Donald Trump has nicknamed the Golden Dome.
Canada chose GlobalEye spy plane without knowing military's needs: sources
Topshee defended the choice of the GlobalEye, saying that NATO also plans to acquire it.
The air force, however, is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage and that blind spots are created during turns.
There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.
Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.

The air force also has concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.

items: Canada receives first F-35 jets from U.S., as full order remains under review

blocks.text: The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.
"Every platform has advantages and disadvantages," Topshee said.
He also testified that the modern battlespace is changing rapidly with the introduction of drones and autonomous systems.
To maintain surveillance, the military, Topshee said, would rely on not only the GlobalEye, but also ground-based radar and satellites to get "the full picture."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Police raid fails to locate three stolen Melbourne Cup trophies worth $1m each
articles.summary:
Officers searched a Mount Waverley home in Melbourne after trophies belonging to winning horse Makybe Diva were stolen from Flemington racecourse

A police raid has failed to locate three…

blocks.text: A police raid has failed to locate three Melbourne Cup trophies belonging to champion horse Makybe Diva after a smash and grab at Flemington racecourse.
A Mount Waverley home in Melbourne’s east was raided on Monday evening after thieves smashed their way into a glass display case at the racecourse about 6.30am.
A 36-year-old Malvern East man was arrested at the Solomon Street home.
He was interviewed by police and released, pending summons.
The trophies, which Victoria police says are valued at $1m each, are yet to be recovered.
The cups, won by the history-making mare in 2003, 2004 and 2005, had been on public display at the racecourse, which hosts the Melbourne Cup, since September.
The champion racehorse, which died in February at the age of 27 after a short and sudden battle with a gastrointestinal condition, was “the people’s horse’, former owner Tony Santic told 3AW.
“Hopefully we can get them back in one piece,” Santic said. “It’s more than devastating. I just can’t believe it.
“I just want to try to get them back and hopefully we get them back in one piece.”
The Victorian Racing Club said the theft was devastating.
“Victoria police is investigating a theft incident that occurred at Flemington racecourse [on Monday] morning involving three Melbourne Cup trophies,” it said.
“We are devastated by the incident and are in direct contact with Tony Santic.”

articles.title: United Airlines says issue affecting departing flights has been resolved

blocks.text: World·Updated

United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
The airline's outage on Monday was the latest high-profile technology meltdown

Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. It also said, "There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue."
United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media.

Pilots reported to air traffic controllers that the problem was related to United's system that helps them determine a plane's final weight to ensure it can safely take off. United did not immediately provide details about which of the airlines systems were affected.

A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown.

articles.title: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people
articles.summary:
Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up

Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next…
articles.byline: Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.

In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.
He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment.

Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn.

If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review.

blocks.caption: The London Job Show at the Westfield shopping centre in May. Young people are bearing the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans.  Photograph: Susannah Ireland/The Guardian

blocks.text: Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014. Milburn said that rate could be lowered to 5% by 2036.
However, central to his plan would be a controversial shake-up of Britain’s benefits system to approach the under-25s as wholly separate from the working-age population at large.

Urging the prime minister not to shy away from welfare reform – after Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown over a plan to cut disability benefits amid pressure from Labour MPs – Milburn warned the future of the next generation depended on the government making changes.
At a press conference in London on Tuesday to mark the launch of his report, he is expected to say: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.”
But Milburn also warned that crude benefit cuts would not work, arguing that changes would need upfront investment.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has promised that changes to benefits in response to Milburn’s review would come with a rethink of youth support.  Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

blocks.text: Burnham pledged on Sunday to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment. Writing in the Guardian, he promised that changes to benefits he was considering in response to Milburn’s review would only be accompanied by a “root and branch rethink” of youth support.

At the heart of Milburn’s blueprint would be the creation of an entirely new welfare system for young people, involving tougher eligibility criteria than for older claimants. In exchange, however, there would be a drastic step-change in support to help young people find work.

This would involve some young people with health conditions and disabilities losing access to current benefits, although they would be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment. Those with the most profound health conditions who would be unable ever to work would still get more generous financial support.
To counterbalance the changes, Milburn said upfront investment to create a new “youth opportunity service” in England should be created to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people.

Accountable to regional mayors and local leaders, the service would combine employment, careers, health and practical support. Young people would receive a personalised participation plan and a named adviser, with access to support guaranteed by two new legal guarantees.

blocks.caption: Milburn’s plan involves a new ‘youth opportunity service’ in England to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian

blocks.text: While education, skills and health policies are devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, Milburn will say at the report launch that the underlying principles in his report should also apply.
after newsletter promotion

Analysis in Milburn’s report shows that for every £1 spent on helping young people into work or education, the state spent £25 on youth benefits last year. Under his proposals that figure would be rebalanced to £2 to £1, bringing Britain closer into line with the ratios in other European countries.

The changes will, however, raise fears among some Labour MPs as well as charities and campaigners that slashing youth benefits could result in plunging more young people into poverty, particularly for those who require additional financial support to manage health conditions.

As Milburn prepared to launch his review, backbenchers from the left of the party – including Nadia Whittome, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, John McDonnell, Apsana Begum, Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon – warned in a letter that an entire generation risked becoming disconnected from work and wider society.

“What young people need is not more punishment, but more opportunity,” the signatories wrote, warning that an approach relying on benefit cuts “risks further disenfranchising young people who are already struggling”.

They added: “Placing young people under threat of losing essential financial support does not address the shortage of good-quality jobs, the barriers facing disabled young people, or the lack of meaningful routes into employment.”

blocks.caption: The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said: ‘What is proposed is a new settlement for young people.’ Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PA

blocks.text: In a bid to ease concerns among Labour MPs after last year’s welfare rebellion threatened to rupture the party and arguably began Starmer’s downfall, Milburn held meetings with MPs on Monday alongside the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden.

McFadden told backbenchers: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR. It’s about bringing together the help young people need in one place – treating them as a person not a departmental client.”

Milburn said Britain had faced a Neet problem for 25 years and had never made a plan to end it before. “We are at a fork in the road and half measures will not do. A complete system reset is needed. A lost generation is not inevitable. A work generation is possible.”

Labour has faced fierce criticism from business groups who say its decisions – including tax increases and a rising minimum wage – have added to Britain’s crisis in youth jobs, while the Conservatives and Reform have pushed for a tougher approach on benefits.
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn’s review was “too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state”.

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years,” she said. “Even so, there’s a long road ahead to see if it can get past welfare-loving Labour MPs.”

articles.title: Journalists call for justice after reporter found dead in Mexican coastal city of Acapulco
articles.summary: A Mexican journalist was found dead on Saturday on the outskirts of Acapulco, a popular resort city in the southern Guerrero state, marking the latest in a string of alleged attacks targeting…

image.caption: Journalists and rights activists held a demonstration Monday after the body of Mexican journalist Eduardo Flores Salado was found on Saturday on the outskirts of the coastal city of Acapulco, prompting calls for greater protection for media workers. Mexican authorities are investigating Flores's dea

blocks.text: World·New

A Mexican journalist was found dead on Saturday on the outskirts of Acapulco, a popular resort city in the southern Guerrero state, marking the latest in a string of alleged attacks targeting reporters in the country.
Authorities probing death of Eduardo Flores, who reported on social issues, missing persons

Mexican journalist Eduardo Flores Salado was found dead over the weekend in Mexico's coastal city of Acapulco, intensifying concerns about reporters as the country remains among the world's deadliest for media workers.
His body was found Saturday night in the Canuto Nogueda neighbourhood, according to local authorities, in the outskirts of Acapulco, Guerrero, a popular resort city in southern Guerrero state.
On Sunday, the Guerrero state prosecutor's office said that the case was being investigated as an "aggravated homicide." It did not announce any arrests or provide a cause of death or motive.

Dozens of Flores's colleagues in Guerrero held a demonstration outside of the state attorney general's office on Monday, calling on Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and local authorities to undergo a comprehensive investigation and implement stricter measures to keep journalists and their families safe.

"There is a lot of fear, of course. You have to be courageous to do journalism, to be a journalist in Guerrero," Cristian Zamora, a journalist and director at the Digital Agency, who had been friends with Flores since 2015 and was in attendance at the Monday demonstration.
"Every day, we go out and we don't know if we're going to return. Every day, we say something and we don't know who we're going to bother. We don't have that freedom."
Eduardo Flores was a well-known journalist in Acupulco. (Eduardo Flores/Facebook)
Over nearly two decades, Flores covered missing persons cases, security and social issues, working as a reporter for multiple local outlets.

Most recently, Flores worked with digital news outlet Enfoque Informativo and was well known in Acapulco for his activism within the 2SLGBTQ+ community. He also co-founded tabloid news outlet La Prensa Rosa, which translates to the Pink Press.

Mexico is consistently named one of the most dangerous and deadliest countries in the world for journalists, with Reporters Without Borders ranking the country as the second-most dangerous place for reporters last year, after Gaza.
Journalists indignant over targeted attacks in Mexico
Zamora described Flores as a "great friend, supportive, attentive and polite."
"He was murdered," he told CBC News. "All of us, his fellow journalists, it caused us indignation, anger at what is happening in the country."
Local 2SLGBTQ+ activist Alberto Serna Mogollon said Flores — whom he and other friends called by the common nicknames "Lalo" or "Lalito" — was a vocal member and supporter of the movement.
"That is why we are here: stand in solidarity, asking for justice from the competent authorities," he told CBC News.

A number of international human rights organizations — including London-based advocacy group Article 19 and Amnesty International — have documented that attacks, threats and murders of journalists frequently go unpunished in Mexico.

In a post on X on Sunday, Article 19 said it condemned the alleged murder of Flores, calling on the Guerrero state prosecutor's office to "conduct a prompt, thorough, and impartial investigation ... that considers their journalistic work as a possible motive for the murder and keeps other lines of investigation open."
Article 19 has documented 181 such cases since 2000 in the Latin American country, many of these concentrated in states with a strong presence of organized crime groups.

It also called on the Protection Mechanism for Human Rights Defenders and Journalists, a state-run program meant to help protect journalists and human rights defenders, to assess the risks facing reporters' families and colleagues and to ensure their protection.
The program declined the Associated Press' request for an interview and did not provide comment for this story.
98% of journalist homicides remain unpunished
Last Wednesday, the AP reported on "exposed shortcomings" in the 2012 program meant to safeguard to more than 2,000 individuals, including approximately 500 journalists.

Under the mechanism's framework, each case first undergoes a risk assessment by a governing board, which creates a security plan. It can then provide tailored physical and emergency measures, such as panic buttons, bodyguards, armoured vehicles and temporary relocation. The mechanism ultimately works alongside federal and state authorities to implement and monitor these protections over time.
Eight journalists were killed while enrolled in the program between 2017 and 2022, according to a joint investigation by Amnesty International and the Committee to Protect Journalists.
Propuesta Cívica, a Mexican civil society organization that provides legal support to journalists and their families, estimates that 98 per cent of journalist homicides remain unpunished.

"The deeper structural problem is that the mechanism has been given a responsibility that belongs to the state as a whole," Vanessa Carrillo, Propuesta Cívica's co-director, told the Associated Press last week.

Cameras, a video recorder, a microphone and placards are placed together on the ground during a protest in July 2023, by journalists to demand justice for the murder of a regional correspondent who was found slain two days prior in, Guadalajara, Mexico. (Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images)
The Inter-American Commission for Human Rights has emphasized that the state must prevent attacks and reduce risks, not simply investigate them.

According to Propuesta Cívica, Mexico's federal Protection Mechanism is hampered by bureaucratic delays, insufficient staffing and a reactive approach. Protection measures are often inadequate, risk assessments delayed and safeguards withdrawn despite ongoing threats.

In 2025, President Sheinbaum said the program could receive additional funding if needed, but Reporters Without Borders said the government has made little progress in fulfilling its press freedom commitments, including a promised review of the program.

items: Violence against journalists in Mexico goes unpunished and ignored

blocks.text: Another reporter death
Flores's death follows that of Roxana Guzman, who directed a Veracruz crime news ​outlet, Pulso Informativo del Sureste.

A video she recorded of masked men breaking down her front door before her abduction on June 2 was widely shared on social media. Her remains were found a month later. Authorities said eight people had been arrested over Guzman's kidnapping and killing, including four municipal police officers from a small town 300 kilometres south.
Flores's employer Enfoque Informativo condemned his death and demanded a thorough and transparent investigation.
"This attack not only takes the life of a colleague, friend, and valuable human being; it constitutes a direct attack on freedom of expression," it said in a statement on Sunday.
"They will not silence us. We will continue to report with the same determination and professional ethics that characterized the work of Eduardo Flores Salado."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC's Tania Miranda Perez, Reuters and The Associated Press

articles.title: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are gaining ground and their advance could have dangerous consequences, writes the BBC's security correspondent.

blocks.text: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden.
Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world.
Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula.

The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears.
Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
In normal times, it accounts for around 12% of global trade, with anywhere between 70 to 150 ships a day making the transit.

But not any more. Although the Houthis say they are no threat to maritime traffic, they are currently at war with Saudi Arabia, making it extremely hazardous for the Saudis to send their oil tankers past the now rebel-controlled coast.
But Mohammed al-Basha, the Yemeni founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, believes the Houthis would struggle to capture the heavily fortified city of Aden.
"Any attempt to seize a densely populated city like Aden would come at a significant human cost," Basha said. "Advancing across the flat coastal plains would also expose Houthi forces to air power."
"For now, the Houthis appear to be seeking a negotiated surrender, hoping to exploit infighting and divisions among southern factions to achieve their objectives without a costly urban offensive."

It is conceivable that the Yemen war will settle into a less dramatic but deeply unsatisfactory stasis - a situation where casualty figures subside yet the country remains split between areas controlled by the Houthis - Iran's Shia allies - and the disparate and often poorly motivated forces of the Saudi-backed Yemeni army.

The former British defence attaché to Yemen, Col Iain Smailes, warned that the recent Houthi advance could trigger a spike in oil prices, as it did when they seized the Bab al-Mandab Strait in September.
He also warns this could have a knock-on effect to security well beyond Yemen's borders.

"By extending their control over the western coastline, the Houthis will increase their ability to smuggle weapons and ammunition from Iran, the Horn of Africa and elsewhere, posing additional threats to the region," Col Smailes said.
"This control will enable both Iran and the Houthis to extend their influence in East Africa and beyond."

articles.title: Third US aircraft carrier brings thousands more troops to Middle East
articles.summary:
The US president oscillates between strike threats on Iran and insisting the war ‘militarily is effectively over’

A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central…

blocks.text: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, US Central Command said in a social media post on Monday, making a dramatic show of military might as Donald Trump keeps his options open for next steps in the Iran war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt brings thousands of additional troops to the Middle East as Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the more than 8-month-old war “militarily is effectively over”.

The Roosevelt, along with its accompanying strike force, left San Diego in September. It joins the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller navy ships, which are in the region to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian shipping.

The HW Bush arrived in the region in April, while the George Washington arrived in August. The navy previously had three carrier strike groups in the Middle East in April, for the first time since 2003.

In addition to the three aircraft carriers, the flotilla in the Arabian Sea now includes 13 destroyers, two cruisers and a littoral combat ship, according to the navy. Two more destroyers are in the Red Sea.

The Roosevelt had deployed along with the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, which includes the USS John P Murtha and USS Anchorage amphibious landing ships and around 2,000 Marines. Those ships have yet to make it to the region.

The third carrier arrived nearly two weeks after midterm elections that saw voters deliver major losses to Trump’s Republican party , driven in part by the unpopularity of the Iran war and its economic effects. The results led JD Vance to publicly break with Trump over the conflict, posting on social media that “the reason we lost is the war”.
Trump has insisted it was the right thing to do and has not ruled out restarting the conflict, which has been locked in a stalemate for months.
Last week, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and that the US was keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate” to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.

Yet, Trump also told reporters last week that he believed it was highly unlikely he would need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over” after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister.

Trump also declared that the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and told Vance – who was a chief negotiator in earlier ceasefire talks – instead to focus on the administration’s domestic anti-fraud campaign targeting Democratic-controlled cities and states.

Negotiations have stalled due to differences over Iran’s nuclear program, an issue that Trump insists be part of any deal meant to end the war. Iran wants the US first to agree to several core conditions, including lifting the naval blockade that is stopping its oil from getting to world markets.
In the meantime, a focal point of the simmering conflict remains the strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war.

Commercial ships are still coming under attack or facing other risks, while the US has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the strait and is helping guide vessels through the contested waters.
Iranian state TV, quoting the naval arm of Iran’s revolutionary guard and the army, warned shipping companies Monday that a US-supported route through the waterway is dangerous because of mines.
Mines have damaged six oil tankers since Sunday, polluting the strait’s coastlines, according to the revolutionary guard’s navy.
Separately, a projectile struck a tanker trying to transit through the strait, starting an engine room fire, but no casualties were reported, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said.
US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, said it has redirected 150 merchant vessels and disabled five since June under the blockade.
Independent assessments from Lloyd’s List, a maritime tracking and analysis firm, show that traffic through the strait remains at less than a third of prewar levels.

articles.title: Gordie Howe bridge surpasses 1M vehicle crossings while other bridges, tunnel lose traffic
articles.summary: The Gordie Howe International Bridge has seen more than a million crossings since it officially opened to vehicle traffic on July 27, according to new numbers from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators…

image.caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge had seen 1,051,470 crossings as of Oct. 31. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor

The Gordie Howe International Bridge has seen more than a million crossings since it officially opened to vehicle traffic on July 27, according to new numbers from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.
Windsor-Detroit tunnel remains the most popular passenger vehicle crossing, CEO says
Meanwhile, vehicle traffic over the Ambassador and Blue Water bridges and through the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel has declined.
The numbers cover the first three full months since the Gordie Howe opened.
They show the bridge averaging around 248,000 passenger vehicle crossings per month and slightly fewer than 85,000 truck crossings.
In a statement, the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority said, too, that more than 48,000 pedestrians and cyclists had used the bridge's multi-use path.

"The Gordie Howe International Bridge supports the efficient and effective movement of traffic in the Windsor-Detroit gateway by providing additional capacity, crossing choice and highway-to-highway connectivity for travellers and commercial operators crossing the border," the statement read.
"We are encouraged by the continued interest in the bridge and the growth in traffic volumes as more users become familiar with the crossing."
Windsor-Detroit Tunnel crossings were down just shy of 19 per cent between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31, while crossings at the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia were down approximately 12.5 per cent.
The Ambassador Bridge saw the biggest decline in total crossings — down nearly 32 per cent compared with the same period last year.
Tunnel CEO not surprised by numbers
Most of that decline was in passenger vehicle traffic, not truck traffic.

Truck crossings were off just 8.75 per cent since the same August-through-October period last year, despite hopes among some residents of Sandwich Town that the new bridge would ease traffic congestion on Huron Church Road.
Truck crossings at the Blue Water Bridge were down just over 30 per cent.
Windsor-Detroit Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he’s not surprised by the numbers.
Tunnel CEO Tal Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing. (CBC)

“[The Ambassador Bridge] had a very long runway to negotiate some very favorable deals with different … trucking companies. And obviously they own a decent amount of trucking infrastructure themselves.”

Truck crossings at the Ambassador Bridge remain up 3.85 per cent for the period running from Jan. 1 to the end of October, compared with the same period last year, while overall bridge traffic is down 6.82 per cent over the same time period.
Czudner said he is happy to see the tunnel, which is jointly owned by the cities of Windsor and Detroit, remain the most popular passenger vehicle crossing.
He also said the Windsor side of the operation has lost less traffic than the Detroit side.

“I think what you're finding is there's a lot of the people who work in automotive, manufacturing, healthcare, live in Windsor-Essex, take the tunnel to work, and then they take the Gordie Howe home,” he said.

“From a pricing perspective, that's actually the cheapest way to go. If you sign up for a [tunnel] Nexpress account, it’s the cheapest way to get from Windsor to Detroit. And if you sign up for a Breakaway account with Gordie Howe, that's the cheapest way to get from Detroit back to Windsor.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Heather Kitching reports local news for CBC stations across Ontario and the North. You can reach her at heather.kitching@cbc.ca.
