articles.title: Alberta has tabled a bill for new riding maps. What could a court challenge mean?
articles.summary: Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday. But legal experts say a potential court…

image.caption: Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled Bill 40, the proposed Electoral Divisions Act, in the legislature on Monday. It would repeal the current Electoral Divisions Act, adopting the new ridings as proposed by an independent advisory panel. (CBC News)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday. But legal experts say a potential court challenge could introduce a high level of uncertainty in advance of the next provincial election.
Legal experts say possible challenge could introduce high level of uncertainty
Alberta’s controversial new riding map is one step closer to implementation after Justice Minister Mickey Amery tabled a bill in the legislature on Monday.
But legal experts say a potential court challenge could introduce a high level of uncertainty in advance of the next provincial election, set for Oct. 18, 2027.
Earlier this month, an advisory panel issued a report on Alberta’s electoral boundaries following a government-led process that saw an initial commission’s riding plan discarded.
Among other changes, it proposes expanding a few Calgary ridings across municipal boundaries and establishing a sole urban seat for Lethbridge, along with three hybrid urban-rural seats.

items: Alberta's new riding map skews Lethbridge, Banff, Calgary seats toward UCP, voter data suggests
'Diluted' and 'muddled': Plan to split Lethbridge into 1 urban, 3 hybrid ridings gets blowback

blocks.text: For three decades, updates to these maps, delivered by bipartisan commissions, have been enacted without much fanfare or controversy.

But this go-around has been marked by accusations of U.S.-style “gerrymandering” — a process in which politicians redraw voting lines so as to provide a boost to their own electoral chances — and threats of a possible court challenge from the Opposition NDP on constitutional grounds.
Alberta NDP accuses Smith of ‘Trump-style’ gerrymandering in new electoral map
The governing UCP previously signed off on the new political boundaries. The bill will now be debated in the House, and Amery has said he expects the legislation to pass by the end of the year.
On the possibility of an injunction

Stephen Thiele, a partner at Gardiner Roberts in Toronto, said a court challenge would involve an application to challenge the constitutionality of the bill, likely under Section 3 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which is concerned with voters’ rights.
Parties could ask for an injunction to prevent the bill from taking effect, and to hold the election based on the current ridings that are in place, he said.
“I would assume that government lawyers would argue that this is not the appropriate time for an injunction,” Thiele said.
"The legislation has taken effect. Elections Alberta has already done its work, and spent a lot of money. They would raise that argument."

Such a Charter challenge would zero in on the right to “effective representation,” the legal principle that allows for the balancing of equal-sized voter populations with other factors, like geography.
Thiele said it's not clear whether any challenge — from the NDP or another group — would be successful.

In part citing delays a legal challenge would pose, Elections Alberta chief electoral officer Gordon McClure wrote in a letter in late October that the government should maintain the electoral boundaries currently in place or postpone the next election.

It’s possible that the elections agency may have to prepare for two different scenarios — one in which the new boundaries come into effect and one in which the old ones are in effect, according to Marion Sandilands, a constitutional lawyer and partner at Conway Litigation.
“Whenever Section 3 challenges happen close to an election, it creates a lot of uncertainty about how the election is to be administered,” Sandilands said.

“Any court hearing this kind of challenge, and if it had an injunction request in it, the court would have to take into account how the election can be administered properly … the closer we get to the election, the higher risk it becomes for the running of the election.”

Amery denied McClure’s request to maintain the prior boundaries or postpone the next election, writing in a letter that the province saw “no value” in considering hypothetical judicial outcomes at this time.
“The final electoral boundaries enacted by the Legislative Assembly will constitute the law of Alberta, and Elections Alberta is expected to prepare accordingly,” he wrote.
He went on to say that other Canadian jurisdictions have demonstrated that electoral administrators could implement revised boundaries and administer elections within "substantially shorter periods.”

items: Elections Alberta reveals October referendum cost $84M, receives additional funds from legislature committee

blocks.text: Challenge to come after royal assent: Nenshi
Naheed Nenshi, the leader of the Opposition, reiterated the NDP's “gerrymandering” characterizations on Monday.
“There is still time for the UCP to do the right thing. They can vote against adopting these gerrymandered maps,” Nenshi told reporters.
While he would not detail next steps, Nenshi said “every lawyer knows” that a bill can only be challenged once it has received royal assent.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, meanwhile, has said her government will assemble a legal team to make the case that the new proposed electoral boundaries achieve effective representation.
Brian O’Ferrall, a retired Alberta Court of Appeal justice who led the advisory panel, wrote in an executive summary that he believes the proposals suggested in the report are "not unconstitutional."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Exodus in Poilievre's office as 5 staffers plan departures
articles.summary: Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office,…

image.caption: The departures come as the Conservatives prepare for six byelections in December. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Sources tell CBC News five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit. The departures will leave big gaps in Poilievre's office, particularly in communications and policy.
Directors, senior-level staff informed Opposition leader of plans to leave: sources
Five members of the Opposition leader's office have informed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre they plan to quit, according to sources.
Those leaving their posts include the deputy chief of staff and director of policy, Aaron Wudrick, who informed caucus last week.
Others include director of communications and issues management, Micah Green, and director of media relations Sam Lilly.
Both are taking new jobs with the newly elected British Columbia Conservative government.
Senior policy adviser Andrew Evans and Poilievre's executive assistant Hayley Quipp have also informed the leader of plans to depart.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to share details about the internal workings of Poilievre's office, but Lilly and Green confirmed their departures in statements.
These departures will leave big gaps in the Opposition leader's office (OLO), particularly in communications and policy.

Wudrick is a longtime Conservative and respected by caucus, previously serving as director of domestic policy at the right-leaning Macdonald-Laurier Institute. Before that, he was the federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.
He was one of the architects of the party's platform in the 2025 election campaign and has served in OLO for two-and-a-half years.

He was recently promoted to deputy chief of staff. His resignation follows other high-level departures from Poilievre's office earlier this year, including former chief of staff Ian Todd and former director of communications Katy Merrifield.
In an email sent to caucus last week, Wudrick said he would be leaving his role effective Nov. 27 for a job in the private sector in a bid to spend more time with his family.

"It has been an honour and a privilege to serve our leader and this team the last 2.5 years," he wrote, adding that he believes the goal of electing Poilievre to be prime minister "remains achievable in the next election."
Evans has been senior policy adviser since 2024, and previously held roles as a staffer in the Ford government. He was assigned to the immigration file, which has been a focus of the Opposition.
Green and Lilly are Poilievre's office's most senior communications staff. Green replaced Merrifield in April, but has been at OLO in a communications role since December 2022.
His LinkedIn page says he's been working for the Conservatives, either at OLO, the party or through an MP's office, since 2019.

Lilly is a longtime figure on Parliament Hill. He's been in communications with OLO since April 2021, starting as a press secretary and rising to director of media relations. In the 2019 election, he was a candidate for the Conservatives in Edmonton Strathcona.
These departures come as Poilievre faces pressure to keep seats in upcoming byelections after losing nine MPs since the 2025 election.

So far, he has lost four MPs to floor-crossing and four others have either announced plans to resign or have already resigned. Another MP, Quebec's Richard Martel, was appointed to the Senate. He still serves in the Conservative caucus.

items: Carney calls December byelections for 6 ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan

blocks.text: There are six byelections in December.. The Conservatives are incumbents in two: Ontario's Brantford-Brant South and Saskatchewan's Yorkton-Melville.

Both seats were previously considered safe for the Conservatives, but the Carney Liberals' high polling in Ontario could see a fight in Brantford-Brant South, which was vacated by former justice critic Larry Brock.
Brock endorsed a local pastor, Dave Carrol, to succeed him — but the party chose Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis. Carrol later chose to run as an Independent, which risks splitting the Conservative vote.

items: Conservatives criticized over appointment of Brantford, Ont., Mayor Kevin Davis to run in byelection

blocks.text: Online posts and local news reports show Poilievre has been spending time in the riding, including this weekend, in a bid to shore up support.
Conservative sources who have spoken to CBC News in the past say, despite challenging polls, there is no plan to try to remove Poilievre and that he has the support of caucus.
Poilievre sailed through his last leadership review in January with 87.4 per cent of the vote from party members.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
articles.summary: Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

image.caption: Philippe Diallo is the third candidate for FIFA's presidency.Image: Bruno Bebert/Bestimage/IMAGO

blocks.text: French federation chief Philippe Diallo was "unanimously" backed by UEFA to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chiefGianni Infantino growing.
European football's governing body said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, with UEFA's "full support" behind the Frenchman.
Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.
Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support of five of FIFA's 211 member associations, before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

blocks.caption: Gianni Infantino seeks another term as FIFA presidentImage: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Son of boxer, head of French football
Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the French Football Federation (FFF), is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.
He was appointed as FFF president in 2023 after being elected with a large majority. He was reelected in 2024 for another four-year term.
Back in September, Diallo said the FFF withdrew its support of Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying the trust in the FIFA President "has been betrayed."
"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said about the decision.
The Frenchman could become FIFA's first black president, while also being the organization's third head from France, after first president Robert Guerin and third president Jules Rimet.

blocks.caption: FIFA will hold the vote for its next president in MarchImage: Ennio Leanza/EPA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Embattled Infantino
Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.
He has been facing growing criticism since his plan of selling parts of the World Cup to private investors. The criticisms were led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan, but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US trying to gather evidence, ahead of potentially complaining to Swiss authorities about alleged "criminal mismanagement" by Infantino.
FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.
Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round of 16 game against Belgium despite being shown a red card in the previous game.
The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.
FIFA wanted a World Cup without politics — it got Trump

articles.title: Failed UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal
articles.summary:
Home Office plans condemned as ‘distressing’ by refugee charities

Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible…

blocks.text: Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow Immigration Enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.

Currently, enforced returns for rejected claimants can only take place after a minimum notice period of five working days, which can allow people to launch other legal interventions or prepare themselves for removal.
Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, condemned the change.
“We must treat people with dignity. Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety,” he said.

“We also need to look at the evidence of what works. The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns. If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer.”

Louise Calvey, the executive director at Asylum Matters, said: “People deserve a fair chance to make their claim for help and sanctuary, but forcibly removing people from the country so they don’t get a chance to make their claims won’t fix that.

“Right now, 63% of the population don’t have access to an asylum legal aid provider. What that means is people are attempting to navigate a horrendously complex and hostile system in a new country, often in a second language. In that environment, many people may not have had the proper advice in initial claims, so many who make further claims are found to have a genuine need for support.
“Expelling people from the country to ensure we never get to hear their legitimate claims is nothing to be proud of – it will lead to real injustices.”
Mahmood has tabled an amendment to the immigration and asylum bill that will scrap the five-day timeframe.
Officials would instead be given a six-month period to remove failed asylum seekers and rejected migrants before further notice is required, the Home Office said.
The changes follow a similar approach to the system that Denmark successfully operates, the Home Office has claimed.
The number of migrants awaiting removal in Denmark was cut from more than 2,185 cases at the end of 2020 to fewer than 1,000 at the end of 2025.

The UK has increased the number of removals since Labour came to power, but faces huge backlogs in asylum applications. As of 30 June 2026, 40,168 people were waiting for an initial asylum decision in the UK. The number of refused applications hit more than 90,000 in the same month, breaking previous records.

There are currently exceptions to the five-day notice period for removals, such as where the removal was disrupted by the individual or was cancelled due to bad weather. In these scenarios, removal can be attempted again without further notice for 21 days.
This timeframe will now be increased to six months under reforms in the bill, which returns to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading on 17 November.

The bill will also introduce a new immigration appeals authority with the aim of speeding up removals and changes to how human rights and modern slavery laws are applied to asylum applications to root out what the government described as “vexatious” claims.
Ministers hope the bill will bring into force proposals that will create a firm but fair asylum system, and which will reduce the pull factors driving illegal immigration.
Under other reforms, the responsibility to make modern slavery decisions for children will be devolved to local safeguarding partners.
This will ensure professionals who already support the child, and are closest to the child, are making the decisions for their future, the Home Office said.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said: “This government is ramping up removals of those with no right to be here, with over 80,000 illegal migrants and foreign nationals returned since the general election.
“Now we are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.”

articles.title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
articles.summary:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm…

blocks.text: Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
Ministers have come under growing pressure to end the NHS in England’s relationship with Palantir, which is run by the Donald Trump-supporting US tech billionaire Peter Thiel.

James Frith, a health minister, said Palantir’s role would end in 2029 to boost public trust in NHS tech, end its “over-dependence” on one supplier and let UK companies start providing crucial digital infrastructure. The DHSC will in the meantime select UK tech firms to replace it.
However, Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs criticised Palantir being given a further two years.

“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS,” said Chi Onwurah, the chair of the Commons science and technology select committee.
“It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier.
Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat MP, said: “After months of campaigning by the Liberal Democrats, the government has finally admitted that the Palantir contract has to end.

“However, ministers have kicked the can down the road to March 2029. That leaves a company co-founded by Trump ally Peter Thiel, and criticised by human rights groups over its work with ICE [the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency], holding the keys to our health data for years to come.”
Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have been urging ministers to activate the break clause in February in the contract that NHS England agreed with Palantir in 2023.

Many NHS care trusts have declined to use the FDP, amid widespread doubts in the service that it is as good as Palantir insists. NHS England last week deleted a claim from its website that 137 trusts were benefiting from the FDP after the Guardian disclosed that 29 were using it never or rarely.

“The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end,” Frith told MPs. The DHSC will soon invite British tech outfits to bid to be part of whoever replaces Palantir. “A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence,” Frith added in a tacit admission that many hospital bosses and doctors are sceptical about Palantir’s claimed benefits.

Ben Coleman, a Labour member of the Commons health select committee, who last week urged ministers to replace Palantir with a group of British firms, said: “I’m glad the government is ending reliance on a single supplier and shaking off the Palantir albatross. This must be done without disrupting patient care or creating new dependence [on a new single supplier]”.
Amnesty International said the decision was “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up”.
“Doctors and nurses … should never have to work in a health service that partners with a company supporting a military committing genocide.

“Palantir has openly acknowledged supporting Israel’s military in ‘war-related missions’, while Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. ‘First, do no harm’ should apply not just to NHS staff, but to the companies the NHS contracts with,” said Tom Guha, its crisis campaigner.

articles.title: People behind Leave.EU and Vote Leave launch new incarnations of pro-Brexit campaigns
articles.summary:
Andy Wigmore says he wants his Enough Official group to join forces with Michael Gove-backed Stay Out movement

The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension…

blocks.text: The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension and badmouthing – and that was just between the different leave campaigns.

Now as a new incarnation of Dominic Cummings’ Vote Leave looks set to re-enter the political fray, so too does a rival anti-EU campaign from the team behind Leave.EU, who ran their own unofficial campaign backed by Nigel Farage.
This time, both have vowed to be cordial with each other, but in 2016 there were significant creative differences.

Many of the names are the same. Oliver Lewis, a veteran of Vote Leave who was a Brexit negotiator under Boris Johnson, will chair Stay Out, a new campaign group backed by the former cabinet minister Michael Gove and under the interested eye of Cummings, though he has no formal role.

The launch of the campaign video – which claimed the costs of rejoining the EU would be £750m a week, and featured footage of recent riots in France and Spain and warnings about unchecked migration – caught No 10 off-guard.

On Monday they were joined by the launch of a parallel campaign from Andy Wigmore’s Leave.EU, which will be called Enough Official. Wigmore told the Telegraph he wanted to work with Lewis’s group. “There’s no split camps this time,” he said. “We’re all going to support each other, and we will support anyone who’s going to fight this.”

A number of high-profile political figures seem to be willing to re-enter the fray from retirement, including Johnson. The former prime minister and leave campaigner told the Telegraph it would be “madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority … [Andy Burnham] won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

Johnson hinted to the paper that he would be willing to be part of a campaign to stay out of the bloc. “There are plenty of people who are only too happy to make the points I’ve made – but I will of course make the points that I’ve made,” he said.

One senior campaigner said it was an irresistible opportunity for many former political advisers who were now out of Westminster politics. “They’re very effective guys that have been sitting around waiting for a chance to make themselves useful. A lot of talent on the right is currently off making money or kicking their feet. Rejoining is the one thing that will bring them back,” they said.
Veterans of both Vote Leave and Leave.EU are split between those who are willing to campaign to stay out and others who believe the political landscape is now far more uncertain.

One senior figure said they “had PTSD” from the Brexit period and vowed to steer clear. “I think that is exactly the reason why the prime minister should not be reopening this debate, but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusion it would be an easy win for either side.”

Another campaign veteran said both pro- and anti-EU campaigns would find it more difficult to get businesses to pick a side or to get public figures involved. “I think that many are scarred from previous involvement, but this would work in both directions,” they said.
Several of those involved in the campaigns said they expected serving politicians to be kept at arm’s length – including Farage.

At a press conference on Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said she would not engage with campaigning on Brexit. “We need to stop obsessing about Europe and whether to be in or out, and actually get on with doing the things that we are elected to do,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
“Sort out the economy, fund our defence, cut welfare, get jobs for people, make sure that businesses can create those jobs. We don’t need to be in the EU to do any of that.”

Badenoch said she believed that voters would decide to stay out of the EU, but added: “I’m not interested in engaging in this debate. They [Labour] want to distract us by making us talk about Brexit, because if we’re talking about that then we’re not talking about the government’s failures. I’m not falling for that trick.”
Launching the campaign over the weekend, Lewis said Stay Out would make the argument on the economics and on immigration – and on the risk of reopening divisions.

“The bloc is also getting bigger, with Albania, Moldova and the western Balkans all in the queue to join, and Brussels wants Britain back in as one of the few countries rich enough to pay for it,” he said. “The country has had enough of arguing about Europe, and it is time to move on and spend our money on our own priorities.”

Gove, who was a co-convener of Vote Leave, said a move towards rejoining would “commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations and a return to the divisions we have spent years putting behind us, at the very moment people are desperate for Westminster to get on with delivering on their priorities.”

Speaking on Monday before a crunch EU summit where Burnham hopes to clinch a new deal with the EU on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the government respected the 2016 result.
“What we’re very focused on is actually what’s in front of us, which is this summit and how we can just help the British people in the situation we face,” he told BBC Breakfast.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy to face retrial next year for deaths of her three children
articles.summary: The 36-year-old's first trial this year fell apart when a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of murdering her three children, will face a retrial next year, a judge has said, after a jury deadlocked last time in a case that gripped the nation.
The judge set a trial date for 29 March 2027, though the district attorney did not explicitly say what charges Clancy would face.
Prosecutors said they wanted a jury trial, and the defence said they took that to mean Clancy, 36, would again face first-degree murder charges.
Five-year-old Cora, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan were strangled at the family home on 24 January 2023. The defence argues she had severe postpartum psychosis.

"I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA [district attorney] that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments, so we will pick a trial date," defence lawyer Kevin Reddington said at Monday's hearing.
Prosecutors wanted a May trial date, but Judge William Sullivan decided on March instead. The judge is due to retire in June.
Clancy was charged in the first trial with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The district attorney has not yet officially said he will proceed with first-degree-murder charges. The BBC has contacted the district attorney's office for comment.

The prosecution could choose to bring lesser charges against Clancy, such as second-degree-murder, which applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without planning.
A week ago, Judge Sullivan rejected a defence attempt to throw out the case on the grounds of double jeopardy.
Double jeopardy is a legal principle that protects someone from being prosecuted more than once for the same crime after an acquittal or conviction.
The judge's decision cleared the way for a second trial. It was Judge Sullivan who declared the mistrial on 4 September because of the hung jury.
Afterwards, some of the 12 jurors said in media interviews that they had been ready to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, but that one juror had held out.
It was not disputed at Clancy's first trial that she strangled the children with exercise bands in the basement of the family home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury.
She had asked her now-ex husband, Patrick Clancy, to leave the house to pick up takeout food and children's medicine shortly before the children were attacked.
The defence team wanted her found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.
The case sparked a debate over how postpartum mental illness is treated in the US.
Clancy is currently in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts.

articles.title: Forensic expert says his analysis raises doubts about how Epstein died
articles.summary: Professor Michael Freeman tells BBC Newsnight that he believes the convicted sex offender's injuries are consistent with a homicide.

blocks.text: This article contains distressing details and references to suicide
A forensic expert has said he believes that convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein's death in prison was the result of a homicide, not suicide.
Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Professor Michael Freeman said that after reviewing the New York City medical examiner's file he believes Epstein was strangled, most likely from behind.

The medical examiner who carried out the autopsy concluded in 2019 that Epstein's injuries were consistent with suicide and there was no evidence of the defensive wounds expected if his death had been a homicide.
Epstein was found dead in prison on 10 August 2019 in New York as he awaited trial on sex trafficking charges.

Dr Barbara Sampson, chief medical examiner at the time of Epstein's autopsy, who ruled that Epstein's death was a suicide, has previously said: "I stand firmly behind our determination of the cause and manner of death for Mr. Epstein." The BBC has approached Sampson for further comment.
Freeman has served as a cause-of-death expert to attorneys-general in the US for death in police custody cases, including George Floyd in Minnesota.

He published his research and the New York City medical examiner's files after presenting his findings at University College London on Monday evening. He obtained the files from Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein.

Freeman, who did not see the body, based his conclusions on the files and photographs from the examiner's report provided to him by Mark Epstein, who has always maintained that his brother was murdered.
Freeman said his analysis is independent and that he was not paid by Mark Epstein.

He told the BBC that he believed there are signs indicating an assault on Epstein, including a deep haemorrhage to his left shoulder and injuries that appear to be consistent to being struck in the face.
Freeman said he believed the evidence was most consistent with strangulation using a ligature and then that same ligature was probably used to suspend the body from the bunk bed.

He said there appeared to be fingernail marks above the ligature mark on Epstein's neck, which "would be consistent with strangulation, particularly from behind. And the attempt by the victim to try to remove the ligature from the neck".
He said "the injuries and the way the body was found don't match up. There's only one remaining explanation then, and that is that the death was as a result of a homicide."

The medical examiner who performed the autopsy at the time told the Department of Justice (DoJ) Office of the Inspector General , externalthat Epstein's injuries were more consistent with, and indicative of, a suicide by hanging rather than homicide by strangulation, adding there was no evidence of defensive wounds consistent with what is seen in victims of strangulation.
Freeman said he would have expected in an investigation of a death by hanging in custody for there to be a photograph before the body was taken down.

According to a DoJ investigation into Epstein's time in prison, the guard who found Epstein immediately called for a second colleague to help, lowered Epstein's body to the floor and began attempts to resuscitate him.
Epstein's death came a month after he was briefly placed on suicide watch, the DoJ report said.
When asked who might have killed Epstein if his interpretation of the evidence was correct, Freeman said he had "no idea".
"That is not something I have an opinion about. That isn't any part of any investigation that I've done," he said.
Epstein was convicted in 2008 of soliciting prostitution from a minor, for which he was registered as a sex offender. He escaped a heavy jail sentence as a result of a plea deal.

Eleven years later, Epstein was charged with running a network of underage girls for sex. He was awaiting trial in 2019 when he was found dead at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City.

articles.title: EU sanctions Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia's richest woman
articles.summary: Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, has been the target of Ukrainian attacks for its role in supplying the Russian military. The EU has now frozen its owner's assets and banned her from…

image.caption: Both Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim and the Kremlin deny the company is involved in Russia's war in Ukraine, Kyiv sees things very differentlyImage: Sergei Fadeichev/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union added Russia's wealthiest woman, online retailer Wildberries' CEO and owner Tatyana Kim, to its Russian sanctions list on Monday.
Kim's EU assets will be frozen as a result and she is barred from making financial transactions in or traveling to the bloc.
Kim, born in Grozny, Chechnya, to ethnic Korean parents, has an estimated net worth of $8.1 billion (€7.4 billion).
The sanctions were part of a larger regime targeting some 50 banks and oil export enablers and nearly 100 business leaders, propagandists and a major pro-Russian hacking group.

EU authorities say they targeted ​Kim due to the fact that Wildberries is "one of the largest taxpayers" in Russia and "operates as a supply network ​for the Russian military by facilitating the sale of military and ​dual-use ‌goods."
An EU statement went on to say that "Kim is supporting, materially or financially, and benefiting from Russia's military and industrial complex."
Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce retailer.
Why is the EU targeting an online retailer?

In its defense against invading Russian forces, Ukraine expanded its military target list this summer to include Wildberries warehouses inside Russia, saying the company's product list — which includes night-vision goggles, ammunition pouches and helmets alongside ‌regular clothing, cosmetics and electronics — is supporting Russia's illegal war.
Kim defended her company at the time, saying its offerings were no different than other online retailers like Amazon in the US and Alibaba in China.
The Kremlin, too, denied that the company and its warehouses were involved in the war effort.
Why Ukraine is targeting Russia's biggest online retailer
Who else is on the EU's newest sanctions list?
In a statement, Wildberries said Brussels' sanctions would have no impact on the company since it has no assets in the bloc nor does it conduct business there.
Other entities on Monday's sanctions list include firms in China, Oman, the Seychelles and the United Arab Emirates linked to the sale of oil from Russia's so-called shadow fleet of illicit tankers.
The sale of that oil also fuels Russia's invasion, which the EU is seeking to hamper through sanctions as well as direct financial and military assistance for Kyiv.

Brussels has imposed more than 20 sanctions packages in response to Russia's February 24, 2022, invasion of Ukraine, targeting thousands of individuals and companies to pressure President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the assault.
The 27-nation bloc intends to introduce another sweeping sanctions package by year's end.
Oil smuggling via Russia's shadow fleet raises concerns

articles.title: Pakistan: Former leader Khan pleads for medical care
articles.summary: Imran Khan appealed to judges to be treated "before it's too late." His wife was also included in the request.

image.caption: Imran Khan says the accusations against him are politically motivatedImage: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former PakistanPrime Minister Imran Khan appealed to the country's Supreme Court in a bid to receive urgent medical attention for himself and his wife.

According to an open letter conveyed to the court through Khan's lawyer, the former leader's doctors had warned him of a risk for brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest and that his blood pressure had risen sharply.
He also said his wife Bushra Bibi required further eye operation, and that she is at risk of losing her eyesight should she not be granted the surgery.
The letter was released to the public by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar.
"Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” the letter reads, asking the judges to give him "justice" before it was too late.
"I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," Khan wrote.
Government contests account
An earlier court order ordered Khan's transfer to a hospital in Pakistani capital Islamabad, with Khan alleging that the authorities had not implemented it.
However, cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said Khan was receiving medical care, while also receiving food and books of his liking.
According to Chaudhry, the former leader has been taken to medical examinations at a hospital in Islamabad eight times, with his health and blood pressure being found to be in order.
Still a popular figure

Despite being in prison since 2023 for corruption offenses, Khan is still considereda popular figure in Pakistan, with his party demanding his release. His wife is alo serving jail time for graft offenses.
Khan argues the charges against him are politically motivated, which the government denies.

The government, led by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, also denied Khan was in solitary confinement. More than 900 visits to Khan have been registered since he started his jail time in 2023, according to the authorities.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan is still a popular figure in PakistanImage: PPI/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a previous case, Khan's attorney told the court that his client had lost about 85% of his right eye's vision. However, his sister later said his situation was improving.

articles.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment
articles.summary:
Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis

In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly…

blocks.text: In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly one million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.

The Labour grandee, who had held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions. Many Labour MPs bristled.

Just six months earlier they had mounted a successful rebellion to kill off the government’s planned £5bn cuts to health and disability benefits, significantly damaging then prime minister Keir Starmer’s political authority by forcing him into a major U-turn on his flagship welfare bill.

That day in the gym, Milburn knew he would have to win over a party suspicious of his motives and anxious about the impact of changes on vulnerable people, even if some acknowledged the growing welfare bill was unsustainable.

On the eve of publishing his report on Tuesday, early signs are that he has assuaged backbench nerves, succeeding where Starmer failed in moving the Overton window within the Labour party on the welfare debate around the young.

Milburn’s strategy was clear from the off: make the moral argument for change, make it loudly and make it often. His favourite – and oft-repeated – statistic has been that the government spends 25 times as much on benefits for young people as it does on supporting them into work.

blocks.caption: Meg Hillier, who had fronted the previous rebellion over welfare reform, indicated Milburn’s proposals should get a ‘fair wind’. Photograph: Jill Mead/The Guardian

blocks.text: In a series of interviews and MP engagement sessions over the following months, he described the projections – that numbers could reach 1.25 million by the early 2030s without major intervention – as a “national failure” that would result in a “catastrophic” generational fault line.

After his interim report in May, he gradually signalled that overhauling health and disability benefits for young people would be a central outcome of his review, suggesting the welfare system in its current form had failed them and was exacerbating inactivity.

Labour MPs were given time to get used to the idea and to air the arguments in public, with controversial elements of the report released early: the abolition of health benefits for under-25s, including existing claimants, among them.

“Alan didn’t want any nasty surprises. He wanted to engage fully with MPs and charities and anybody else with concerns. The government can’t move forward on this unless it’s able to bring people with them,” said one government source.
after newsletter promotion

He had several factors working in his favour. As his days in No 10 ran out, Starmer was so weakened that Milburn was able to “bulldoze” Downing Street into supporting his proposals, according to another source, especially as Pat McFadden, the welfare secretary, was already on board.
Secondly, several of the leading figures in the welfare rebellion were now inside government – most notably Louise Haigh, who is now Andy Burnham’s number two, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Meg Hillier, the moderate chair of the Treasury select committee who had fronted that rebellion, last week indicated the proposals should get a “fair wind”, although she also acknowledged the difficulty of the choices ahead.

Thirdly, the drip-drip of pitch-rolling came alongside a wider sense of alarm in the UK over the prospects of the next generation, amid concerns over rising mental ill health, worries over social media and AI upending the jobs market.

Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill “as soon as we possibly can”, but has warned against “crude cuts” (which the government would struggle to get past Labour MPs anyway) in the push for “sustainable” employment.

His approach has echoes of Tony Blair, who talked of “a hand up, not a hand out”, actively pursuing a policy of reforming and investing in welfare specifically to bring down what he termed the “bills of social failure”.

The big difference now is that the fiscal backdrop is more challenging, though Milburn will recommend that ministers spend hundreds of millions on back-to-work support in the short term in return for welfare savings, increased tax receipts and a fairer, happier country over the long-term.

The rather clunky symbolism of choosing a boxing gym for his first promotional visit last year wasn’t lost on anybody. Since then, Milburn – a former chair of the Social Mobility Commission – has been clear this is a fight he thinks the government needs to have.

His recommendations, along with those from the Timms review into health and disability benefits, which will be published in coming weeks, will form the basis of a white paper next spring which will then become a new welfare bill, voted on by Labour MPs.

So for now, the campaign to win them over continues. Standing alongside Milburn at a meeting of the parliamentary party on Monday night, McFadden said: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia challenged by Yemeni allies over ceding ground to Houthis
articles.summary:
Strategy of redeploying forces to try to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden comes as Islamist group makes steady gains

Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.
The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.
The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.
The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.

He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Saudis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”

The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

articles.title: Trump departs for Philippines to attend ASEAN summit
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday (November 16) for a trip to Asia that includes an ASEAN summit in the Philippines and a visit to China, where he said he might meet North…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 17, 2026 2:58am
US President Donald Trump gestures, as he boards Air Force One en route to Manila, Philippines, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, US, November 16, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria

US President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday (November 16) for a trip to Asia that includes an ASEAN summit in the Philippines and a visit to China, where he said he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also joined Trump on the trip, boarding Air Force One with him at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
Speaking to reporters before his departure, Trump said a possible meeting with Kim would take place in China and depend on Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump also said he expected to meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin during the trip, with potential discussions covering Russia's war in Ukraine, nuclear nonproliferation and the war in Iran. — Reuters

articles.title: 120-year-old church bell weighing 300 pounds stolen from belfry in rural Manitoba
articles.summary: The case of the stolen church bell has police sounding an alarm — and scratching their heads.

image.caption: The bell stolen from the Sacred Heart of Jesus church is estimated to weigh more than 130 kilograms. RCMP don't know how or when the bell was removed from the tower. (Submitted by RCMP)

blocks.text: Manitoba
The case of the stolen church bell has police sounding an alarm — and scratching their heads.
Damage seen at top of belfry but RCMP unsure how heavy bell removed

A bell estimated to weigh 300 pounds (about 136 kilograms) was somehow removed from a wooden belfry at the Sacred Heart of Jesus Ukrainian Catholic Church, about 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg near Fraserwood, Man.
RCMP don't know how or when it was removed.
"It's still a bit of a mystery," RCMP Const. Merry Ploeg told CBC Monday, adding the bell is unique.
"It's brass, [and] it's got some ornate designs, including a rosary," she said, adding it also has an image of the sacred heart surrounded by a crown of thorns, crucifix and an anchor.
"We would really appreciate the public being kind of aware of it and on the lookout."
The theft was reported Saturday, RCMP said in a Monday news release.
Rev. Andriy Rabiy, auxiliary bishop of the Archeparchy of Winnipeg — which oversees Ukrainian Catholic churches in Manitoba — said he felt "great disbelief and shock" when he heard what happened.
"Sometimes we hear about break-ins into those kind of abandoned churches … [with] some small things being taken," he said.
"But not to that degree."
Rabiy said Sacred Heart of Jesus is one of two Ukrainian Catholic parishes in the Fraserwood area, with a history that goes back to when the first Ukrainians arrived in Manitoba.
Damage can be seen at the top of the wooden belfry. (Submitted by RCMP)
The number of parishioners has dwindled as people have left farming communities, he said, and the church is now mainly used for special occasions like funerals or annual liturgy services.
But those who remain in the community care deeply about the building, said Rabiy.
"Many of those churches actually kind of … stand as a witness to the past history that they had," Rabiy said.
"I can only imagine what kind of ache, of pain people experience," he said, adding that there is at least one person offering a $500 reward for any information that could help get the bell back.
Scrap dealers notified to watch for bell: RCMP
The wood-clad belfry is about 1½ storeys tall and stands on its own at the back of the church in Manitoba's Interlake region, about 12 kilometres northwest of Gimli.
The RCMP officers who investigated the theft found noticeable damage to the top of the belfry, police said in Monday's news release.
Ploeg didn't want to speculate on why someone would take the bell, but said the only thing RCMP can think of is that someone might try selling it for scrap metal.
"We've actually contacted all the scrap metal and recycling businesses in the area, including in Winnipeg, and notified them to be on the lookout for this bell specifically," Ploeg said.

The Manitoba Historical Society says the belfry was imported from Switzerland when the original church was built in 1906. That church was destroyed by fire in 1940, and the present church was built in 1942.
The bell is also from Switzerland and came at the same time, RCMP said.
The small church is a mission of the much larger Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in Gimli.

items: Church bell and memorial plaques stolen from oldest surviving Ukrainian Catholic Church in Canada

blocks.text: Ploeg said the parishioners are extremely concerned, as is she, by the fact someone went to such lengths to take the bell.
"Should the other churches be maybe … [be] looking at getting security footage or more regularly checking their properties?" she said.
"Everybody involved is very invested in seeing the bell returned. I'm really hoping that we can get it back and that it isn't scrap."
RCMP are asking anyone who has any information about the theft or noticed anything suspicious in the area over the last week to contact them at 204-642-5106.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.
With files from Tyler Searle

articles.title: Grammy Awards: Raye and Rosalia lead nominations
articles.summary: The nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards are in and women dominated the top categories for the highest accolade in the music industry.

image.caption: Raye received 11 Grammy nominationsImage: Mike Gray/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: British singer Raye, with the genre mixing hit "Where Is My Husband!," landed at the top of the list of Grammy Award nominees on Monday, followed by Spanish musician Rosalia and "Choosin" Texas" artist Ella ‌Langley.
Raye earned 11 ⁠Grammy ⁠nominations including nods for song and record of the year for "Husband," and for album of the year for "This Music May Contain Hope."
She now ties Beyonce's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
For her part, Rosalia received nine nominations, just days after sweeping the Latin Grammys with ​her album "Lux."

blocks.caption: Rosalia mixes genres such as flamenco and popImage: Julie Sebadelha/AFP

blocks.text: First-time nominee Langley secured seven, as did Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers.
Megastar Taylor Swift received five nominations.
Only one male artist nominated for Best Album

Besides Raye, competitors in the album race include Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl," Langley's "Dandelion," Rosalia's "Lux," Bridgers' "Lost Weekend," Olivia Dean's "The Art of Loving," and Rodrigo's "you ​seem pretty sad for a girl so in love." Bruno Mars was the only male artist nominated in the category, for his album "The Romantic."

blocks.caption: Taylor Swift, has taken the album of the year trophy a record four timesImage: Caroline Brehman/REUTERS

blocks.text: The record of the year category is made up of Dean's “Man I Need,” Langley's “Choosin' Texas,” Mars' “I Just Might,” Raye's “Where Is My Husband!”, Rodrigo's “The Cure,” Rosalía’s “Berghain” featuring Björk and Yves Tumor, Swift's “The Fate of Ophelia” and Tame Impala and Jennie's “Dracula.”

K-pop sensation ⁠BTS declined to submit any ​music for consideration in protest over a new Asian pop music category. Members of the South Korean band said they did not believe music should be categorized by region.

blocks.caption: K-pop powerhouse BTS said in July they are not interested in winning a new Asian music categoryImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dolly Parton, the country legend who died in August, received three posthumous nominations.
Winners will be announced on February
The final Grammy voting round will run from December 10 to January 7, with winners selected by around 16,000 Recording Academy members.
Winners will be announced at a red-carpet ceremony in downtown Los Angeles ‌on ​February 7.
The event will be broadcast live on Walt Disney's ABC and streamed on Disney+ and Hulu.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth
articles.summary: When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into…

image.caption: Voyager 1: Destined to wander the Milky Way "eternally"Image: NASA/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.
Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.
NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.
But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.
Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.
It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.
How did Voyager 1 get so far and where is it going?
In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.
On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.
In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.
That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.
Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

blocks.caption: There were two Golden Records, one on Voyager 1 and another on Voyager 2, a second spacecraft on the same 1970s mission. They were protected with this gold aluminum cover.Image: United Archives/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voyager 1 is an ongoing scientific experiment
The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.
"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.
Something you didn't already know about Voyager 1
No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.
We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.
